Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/distribution.md

# Building and distributing

`mygo build` turns a project into apps people install: an app bundle and a
disk image on macOS, an executable and an installer on Windows, an
executable, a desktop entry, an archive with its install script and a Debian
package on Linux.

```sh
bun run build        # mygo build, in a project with a web frontend
go tool mygo build   # in a project of native UI
```

It:

1. with a web frontend, writes the TypeScript client, so the frontend
   builds against the Go code, and runs `buildCommand` from the
   configuration, which builds the frontend into `frontendDist`;
2. compiles the app, with the frontend embedded when there is one, for
   production: without the web inspector, and with the name, identifier
   and version of the configuration linked in;
3. packages it for each platform in `build/<os>-<arch>/` (`out` in
   the configuration);
4. signs what it can, and with [updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md) configured, writes the
   signed update archives, and delta updates from the published versions.

## Platforms

`-platform` lists `GOOS/GOARCH` targets, by default the machine's own:

```sh
mygo build -platform darwin/universal,windows/amd64,windows/arm64,linux/amd64,linux/arm64
```

`darwin/universal` combines arm64 and amd64 in one app. MyGo needs no cgo,
so any machine compiles for every platform. Some steps need the tools of a
platform, and are skipped with a note elsewhere: macOS apps are signed and
put in disk images on macOS only, and Windows installers are made on other
systems only where [NSIS](#the-installer) is installed.

The CLI defaults to `CGO_ENABLED=0`. If an app's dependencies need cgo,
set `CGO_ENABLED=1` in the environment for `mygo dev`, `mygo build` and
`mygo generate`. Those builds need a C compiler for the target platform;
when cross-compiling, set `CC` to a suitable cross compiler.

| Platform | In `build/<os>-<arch>/`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| macOS    | `My App.app`, signed, and `my-app-0.1.0-arm64.dmg` (`my-app-0.1.0.dmg` for `darwin/universal`), with [updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md) also `install.sh`                                                                                  |
| Windows  | `My App.exe`, the files of the app, and the installer `my-app-setup-0.1.0-amd64.exe`, with [updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md) also [`install.ps1`](#install-scripts-for-macos-and-windows)                                                 |
| Linux    | `my-app`, `my-app.desktop`, `my-app.png`, `my-app.xml` for the file types the app defines, the files of the app, their archive `my-app-0.1.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz` with [`install.sh`](#the-install-script), and the Debian package `my-app_0.1.0_amd64.deb` |

Other flags: `-debug` keeps development features such as the inspector,
`-skip-dmg` and `-skip-notarize` skip those steps, `-sign` overrides the
signing identity of macOS, and `-o` the output directory. See
[the CLI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/cli.md#mygo-build).

## Name, icon and version

The configuration describes the app:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  name: "My App",
  identifier: "com.example.myapp",
  version: "1.2.0",
  copyright: "© 2026 Example Inc.",
});
```

* `name` is what users see: the app bundle, the executable, menus, the
  installer.
* `identifier` is a reverse DNS name unique to the app. Systems key
  preferences, permissions and registrations on it: keep it once released.
* `version` is the app's version, which `App.Version()` returns and
  [updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md) compare.

The icon is `resources/icon.png`, or the `icon` of the configuration: a square PNG,
ideally 1024×1024. `mygo build` makes it the `.icns` of macOS, the icon
resource of the Windows executable and the icon of the Linux desktop entry.
Beside it, the same name with `-dev` (`resources/icon-dev.png`) is the icon
of the development app that `mygo dev` builds, when it exists, to tell it
from the app in the Dock or the taskbar; it does not ship with the app.

On macOS, `macos.icon` adds an asset catalog, which macOS prefers to the
`.icns`: an `Assets.car` compiled with `actool`, whose app icon is named
`AppIcon` (or what `macos.infoPlist` sets as `CFBundleIconName`), or an
Icon Composer `.icon`, the layered icon of macOS 26, which `mygo build`
compiles with `actool` from Xcode 26 or later, with the `.icns` that
`actool` renders from it in place of the PNG's. Building elsewhere, or when
the compilation fails, skips the `.icon` with a message, and the app keeps
the PNG's `.icns`. `mygo dev` shows the `.icns`.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  macos: { icon: "AppIcon.icon" }, // outside resources, which ship as they are
});
```

For builds without Xcode, such as CI on Linux, commit the `Assets.car`
that `actool` compiles from the `.icon` and make it `macos.icon`. The
`.icon` has to be named `AppIcon.icon`: `actool` names the icon after the
file, and compiles nothing when `--app-icon` differs.

```sh
mkdir -p icon
xcrun actool AppIcon.icon --compile icon --platform macosx --target-device mac \
  --minimum-deployment-target 12.0 --app-icon AppIcon \
  --output-partial-info-plist icon/partial.plist
```

This writes `icon/Assets.car`, for `macos: { icon: "icon/Assets.car" }`.

## Resources

Files the app reads at run time, such as a database seed, a helper binary
or the images of a tray icon, ship with it. Everything in the `resources`
directory of the project is copied into the app, as are the files and
directories listed in `resources` in the configuration, under their base names:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  resources: ["third_party/licenses", "bin/helper"],
});
```

At run time `App.Path(mygo.PathResources)` is where they are:
`Contents/Resources` in a macOS app, the executable's directory elsewhere,
and the project's `resources` directory under `go run` and `go test`:

```go
dir, _ := mygo.App.Path(mygo.PathResources)
seed := filepath.Join(dir, "seed.db")
```

`mygo dev` copies them into the development app too, and rebuilds it when
they change. Hidden files are left out.

### Platform resources

Some resources belong to one platform, such as a program built for one
system and processor. Directories of `resources` named after a platform
hold them, laid out like `resources` itself:

```
resources/
├── data/seed.db                    every app
├── darwin/                         macOS apps
├── darwin-arm64/bin/server         macOS on Apple silicon
├── darwin-amd64/bin/server         macOS on Intel
├── linux-amd64/bin/server          Linux on x86-64
├── linux-arm64/bin/server          Linux on ARM64
└── windows-amd64/bin/server.exe    Windows on x86-64
```

They are named like the targets of `-platform`: a system, `darwin`,
`linux` or `windows`, for all of its apps, or a system and an
architecture, as in `darwin-arm64` or `windows-amd64`, for one. An app
ships the platform directories of its target merged with the other
resources, so the Linux x86-64 app above has `data/seed.db` and its own
`bin/server`, and nothing of the other platforms. A path that two
directories would both install fails the build, and so does a directory
named the way other tools name platforms, such as `darwin-x64` or `macos`,
which would ship to every platform. The build also notes a target without
a directory of its own when another architecture of its system has one,
such as `linux/arm64` next to `linux-amd64`.

A universal macOS app (`darwin/universal`) ships `darwin` and
`darwin-universal`, and combines `darwin-arm64` with `darwin-amd64`:
every file of one needs its counterpart in the other, programs and
libraries become universal binaries, as `lipo` makes them, and other files
must be identical. Put what serves both architectures, such as programs
that already are universal binaries, in `darwin`.

`mygo dev` ships the platform directories of the machine it runs on.
Under `go run` and `go test`, `PathResources` is the `resources`
directory as it is, platform directories included.

### Helper executables

Programs the app runs, such as a server written in another language or a
tool like `ffmpeg`, are resources too: put the build for each platform in
its [platform directory](#platform-resources) and run it from there.

```go
dir, _ := mygo.App.Path(mygo.PathResources)
cmd := exec.Command(filepath.Join(dir, "bin", "server"))
```

The same code runs `bin\server.exe` on Windows, where `exec.Command`
finds the program of an absolute path without its extension.

`mygo build` signs them with the app, so that Gatekeeper and SmartScreen
accept them and notarization passes:

* On macOS, every Mach-O executable and library among the resources, and
  every app, framework or plug-in bundle holding some, is signed from the
  inside out with `signingIdentity`, with the hardened runtime and a
  timestamp for a Developer ID. Signed ad hoc, the default, only code
  without a signature is signed: Apple silicon runs no unsigned code.
* On Windows, with `certificate` or `signCommand`, every executable and
  DLL among the resources that has no signature is signed. Those signed by
  their publishers keep their signatures.

Under the hardened runtime, some programs need entitlements, such as
`com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` for a JavaScript runtime that compiles
code as it runs. Code keeps the entitlements it was signed with, so the
official builds of such runtimes work as they are, and
`macos.helperEntitlements` gives code entitlements of its own, by its path
in the app's resources, such as `bin/server` for
`resources/darwin-arm64/bin/server`:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  macos: {
    signingIdentity: "Developer ID Application: Jane Doe (TEAMID)",
    helperEntitlements: { "bin/server": "server.entitlements.plist" },
  },
});
```

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit</key>
  <true/>
</dict>
</plist>
```

### Native libraries of packages

A Go package that loads a native library with purego, as the
[terminal plugin](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/plugins/terminal.md) loads libghostty-vt, names its
builds in a `mygo-plugin.json` next to its sources, with a file per
platform, where to download it and its SHA-256:

```json
{
  "libraries": [
    {
      "name": "libexample",
      "files": {
        "darwin-arm64": { "name": "libexample.dylib", "url": "https://…/libexample-darwin-arm64.dylib", "sha256": "…" },
        "linux-amd64": { "name": "libexample.so", "url": "https://…/libexample-linux-amd64.so", "sha256": "…" },
        "windows-amd64": { "name": "example.dll", "url": "https://…/example-windows-amd64.dll", "sha256": "…" }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

`mygo build` and `mygo dev` find these files in the packages the app is
built from, download each library once into the user's cache
(`<cache>/mygo/natives/<sha256>/`), check its SHA-256, and install it at
the top of the app's resources under its name, signed like the other
code there; a universal macOS app gets both architectures in one file.
The package loads it from `PathResources`. Building for a platform the
package has no file for fails.

## macOS

`mygo build` makes an app bundle, signs it, and puts it in a disk image
whose window invites users to drag the app to Applications.

### Signing and notarization

Apps signed ad hoc, the default, run on the Mac that built them, but
Gatekeeper blocks them on others. To ship an app, sign it with a Developer
ID of the [Apple Developer Program](https://developer.apple.com/programs/)
and have Apple notarize it:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  macos: {
    signingIdentity: "Developer ID Application: Jane Doe (TEAMID)",
    notarize: { keychainProfile: "notary" },
  },
});
```

Store the credentials of the notary service in the keychain once:

```sh
xcrun notarytool store-credentials notary
```

`mygo build` then signs the app with the hardened runtime, submits the disk
image to the notary service, and staples the ticket to the disk image and
to the app, which updates ship. `security
find-identity -v -p codesigning` lists your identities, and `mygo doctor`
counts the Developer IDs.

### Info.plist and entitlements

`macos.infoPlist` adds keys to the app's `Info.plist`, or replaces MyGo's,
for example the usage descriptions that pages using the camera or the
microphone need:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  macos: {
    minimumSystemVersion: "13.0",
    infoPlist: {
      NSCameraUsageDescription: "Scan documents with the camera.",
      LSApplicationCategoryType: "public.app-category.productivity",
    },
    entitlements: "entitlements.plist",
    dmgTitle: "My App Installer",
  },
});
```

`entitlements` signs the app with a property list of entitlements, and
`helperEntitlements` [helper executables](#helper-executables).
`minimumSystemVersion` is the oldest macOS the app runs on, 12.0 by
default.

### Provisioning profiles

Restricted entitlements, such as Communication Notifications, need a
provisioning profile that authorizes them, including for Developer ID
distribution. Set `macos.provisioningProfile` to its path, relative to the
project or absolute. `build` and `dev` copy it to the bundle's
`Contents/embedded.provisionprofile` before signing, so the signed app,
disk image and update archive contain it.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  macos: {
    signingIdentity: process.env.MACOS_SIGNING_IDENTITY,
    provisioningProfile: process.env.MACOS_PROVISIONING_PROFILE,
    entitlements: "entitlements.plist",
  },
});
```

The profile must match the signing certificate, bundle identifier and
entitlements, including the application and team identifiers. MyGo embeds
it as supplied; it does not create profiles or derive entitlements from
them. Apple validates their authorization when the app runs. A profile
cannot be used with ad-hoc signing (`-sign -`). `dev` signs ad hoc unless
it is given `-sign` (it does not use `macos.signingIdentity`), and its app's
identifier is `<identifier>.dev`, which the app's profile does not
authorize: leave the profile and the restricted entitlements out of
development builds with a [computed configuration](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#computed-configuration),

```ts
export default defineConfig(({ command }) => ({
  macos: {
    signingIdentity: process.env.MACOS_SIGNING_IDENTITY,
    ...(command === "build" && {
      provisioningProfile: process.env.MACOS_PROVISIONING_PROFILE,
      entitlements: "entitlements.plist",
    }),
  },
}));
```

or pass `-sign` and give `dev` a profile for `<identifier>.dev`. It
watches the profile and rebuilds when it changes.

Keep profiles out of version control and provide their paths through the
build environment. See Apple's
[Inside code signing: provisioning profiles](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3125-inside-code-signing-provisioning-profiles).

## Windows

The executable carries the icon, the version information and a manifest
(per-monitor DPI awareness, modern controls), and runs without a console
window. A `.syso` file of your own in the main package replaces them.

### The installer

`mygo build` also makes `my-app-setup-1.2.0-amd64.exe`, named after the
app's [`slug`](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#the-app) and its architecture as the disk
images are, so that the installers of two
targets, uploaded to one release, keep both. It installs the app for
the current user in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\My App`, which needs no
administrator rights and lets the app [update itself](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md), adds a
Start menu shortcut and an uninstaller listed in Settings, and registers
the app's URL schemes and file associations. Its last page offers to run
the app and to create a desktop shortcut, which is checked; silent
installs (`/S`) create none.

The shortcuts, the entry in Settings > Apps and the installer's title
show the app's `name`, or
[`windows.displayName`](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#windows) when the executable and
its folder should keep a plain name, as `weather.exe` in
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\weather` for an app that shows as `天气助手`:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  name: "weather",
  windows: { displayName: "天气助手" },
});
```

Characters that file names cannot hold, such as `:` and `?`, become `-`
in the names of the shortcuts only. The installer of a version that sets
`displayName` replaces the shortcuts that an earlier version made under
the name.

The installer is made with [NSIS](https://nsis.sourceforge.io). On
Windows, `mygo build` uses NSIS when it is installed, and otherwise
downloads it the first time it needs it: the official NSIS 3.13 zip, from
a copy on MyGo's GitHub releases or else from SourceForge, checked against
its SHA-256 and kept in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\mygo`. On macOS and
Linux, install NSIS to make Windows installers (`brew install makensis`,
`apt install nsis`); without it, `mygo build` skips the installer.

### Code signing

Unsigned apps make SmartScreen warn users. Sign the executable, the
[helper executables](#helper-executables), the installer and its
uninstaller with a certificate:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  windows: { certificate: "certs/code-signing.pfx" },
});
```

The password comes from the `MYGO_WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`
environment variable. On Windows `signtool` signs, from the Windows SDK;
elsewhere `osslsigncode`. `timestampUrl` changes the time stamping server,
by default `http://timestamp.digicert.com`.

Certificates on hardware tokens or in cloud services, such as Azure Trusted
Signing, sign with a command of their own, in which `%1` is the file:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  windows: {
    signCommand: "signtool sign /fd sha256 /tr http://timestamp.digicert.com /td sha256 /a %1",
  },
});
```

## Linux

`mygo build` writes the executable, named after the app's
[`slug`](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#the-app), which is its name in lower case by
default, a desktop entry and the icon, and a Debian package, which
installs the app in `/opt/my-app` with its desktop entry, icons, URL
schemes and file types:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  linux: {
    maintainer: "Jane Doe <jane@example.com>",
    comment: "Take notes",
    categories: ["Office"],
    depends: ["libayatana-appindicator3-1"],
    command: "my-app",
  },
});
```

The package depends on GTK 3 and WebKitGTK; `depends` adds more packages.
An app that shows no web page, in a window or a `ui.WebView`, as an app of
[native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md), needs GTK alone: `webview: false` leaves WebKitGTK
out of its package, and out of what `install.sh` and `mygo doctor` (in the
project) check, as the app never loads it.
`maintainer` defaults to the `author` of package.json, else the name of
the app.
`comment` describes the app in its desktop entry and package, and
`categories` places it in application menus (`Utility` by default).
The app opens from the applications menu. `command` also gives it a
command, `/usr/bin/my-app` from the package and `~/.local/bin/my-app` from
[`install.sh`](#the-install-script); without it, neither adds a command,
which leaves the name to a command-line tool of the same name, such as
the app's own.

Keep the slug of a released app. Its Linux files are named after it, and
an update replaces the files of the same names: one to a version with
another slug leaves the old executable in place, which the desktop entry
that `install.sh` registered still runs, and the Debian package of the
new slug is another package, installed next to the old one. Choose the
slug before the first release, as `cloud-music` for `云音乐`, whose own
would be `yun-yin-le`.

### The install script

Every Linux build also gets the app as an archive,
`my-app-1.2.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz`, and `install.sh`, which installs it for
the user without root: the app in `~/.local/my-app.app`, where it can
[update itself](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md), its desktop entry, icon, URL schemes and file
types, and with `linux.command` that command in `~/.local/bin`, unless
another program is there. With
[updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md) configured, it downloads the latest version, which
the update manifest of the machine names, and checks its size and its
Ed25519 signature against `updates.publicKey`, as the app's updater does,
before installing it, so one line installs the app:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/me/my-app/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

With a [`tagPrefix`](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md#set-up) other than `v`, the script of any
release, such as `…/releases/download/desktop-v1.2.0/install.sh`, installs
the newest release tagged with the prefix.

It checks the signature with `openssl pkeyutl -rawin`, which OpenSSL 3.0
and later have (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, Fedora 36, RHEL 9 and later).
Without it, as with OpenSSL 1.1.1, it downloads nothing and says so; the
archive can then be downloaded from the release and given to the script,
which installs an archive it is given, or finds next to it, unchecked.

`-upload` publishes it with the archives; with `updates.url`, publish it
next to the manifests. Next to the archive of its version, as in
`build/linux-amd64/`, it installs that archive instead, and it installs
the one it is given:

```sh
sh install.sh my-app-1.2.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
sh install.sh --uninstall   # keeps the settings and data of the app
```

Running it again installs the version it finds over the installed one.
The app needs WebKitGTK, which `install.sh` does not install: when the
system's library cache has none, it says so after installing, with the
command that installs it on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch and openSUSE,
unless `linux.webview` is `false`.
When the app updates itself, it registers the desktop entry and file types
of the new version, so a version that adds URL schemes or file types gets
them. The Debian package suits people who want the system's package manager to
update the app; `install.sh` suits the others, and is the Linux install
that updates itself.

### Install scripts for macOS and Windows

With [updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md), the same `install.sh` installs the app on
macOS, and Windows builds get `install.ps1`, so one line installs the app
on each system:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/me/my-app/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

```powershell
irm https://github.com/me/my-app/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
```

On macOS, `install.sh` downloads the archive that the update manifest of
the Mac's architecture, else of `darwin-universal`, names (Apple silicon's,
`darwin-arm64`, also from a shell under Rosetta), checks its size
and its Ed25519 signature against `updates.publicKey`, as the app's
updater does (macOS has no tool for Ed25519 signatures, so the script
hashes with `openssl` and `shasum` and does the arithmetic of the curve in
JavaScript for Automation), quits the app if it runs, and replaces the
bundle in `/Applications`, or in `~/Applications` when the user cannot
write to `/Applications` or the app is already there, then opens it. It
never asks for root, and an app of the same name with another bundle
identifier is left alone. `curl` sets no quarantine, so the app opens
without the prompt of Gatekeeper for downloaded apps.
`sh install.sh --uninstall` removes the app and keeps its settings and
data.

`install.ps1` runs in Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7. It
downloads the installer of the latest version for the PC's architecture
(`amd64` or `arm64`), checks its SHA-256 against `SHA256SUMS`, quits the
app if it runs, runs the installer silently (`/S`) in the folder of the
installed version, and opens the app. The installer uninstalls it as
usual, from Settings > Apps.

Builds with updates write `SHA256SUMS`, the SHA-256 of the installers,
archives and scripts in the format of `sha256sum`, to the output
directory, which `-upload` publishes with them, merging the lines of
earlier uploads of other platforms: those of the same GitHub release, or
those of the `SHA256SUMS` that `updates.url` serves for `updates.s3`,
without the files of earlier versions that the upload replaces. It names
the files as the build does; GitHub turns the spaces of uploaded names
into dots, which `install.ps1` follows. With `updates.url` and your own
server, publish the scripts and `SHA256SUMS` next to the manifests, with
the lines of every platform's latest files.

`SHA256SUMS` is not signed: it catches a download that is broken or cut
short, not a release whose files someone replaced. On Windows, sign the
installer ([code signing](#code-signing)) so that Windows shows who made it.

For testing, `MY_APP_DOWNLOAD_URL` (the [slug](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#the-app) of the app in capitals) is
where both scripts download from instead, `MY_APP_INSTALL_DIR` the folder
of the app on macOS, and `MY_APP_NO_OPEN=1` leaves the app closed.

## Languages

An app with [catalogs](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/i18n.md) declares their languages to each system,
its source language first, which the system falls back to:

* macOS: `CFBundleDevelopmentRegion`, `CFBundleLocalizations` and a
  localization folder per language in `Contents/Resources`, named as Xcode
  names them (`de.lproj`, `zh-Hans.lproj`, `zh-HK.lproj` for `zh-Hant-HK`),
  so that AppKit says its own texts (the Services menu, the panels) in the
  language the app shows, and System Settings lists the app's languages.
* Linux: `Name[xx]` and `Comment[xx]` in the desktop entry, by POSIX
  locale (`de`, `zh_CN`, `zh_TW`, `sr@latin`).
* Windows: the installer is in each of the languages, and picks the
  system's; NSIS 3 has files of some 60 languages, and a language it has
  none of stops the build, saying which it has. The file properties have a
  table of strings per language.

The app's name and description in a language are its catalog's
`mygo.appName` and `mygo.appDescription`; the configuration's `name` and
`linux.comment` are those of the source language, and on Windows
`windows.displayName` in place of `name` when it has one. An app without catalogs
declares no languages.

On macOS, the other strings of `Info.plist`, such as the reasons the
system shows as it asks for the microphone or the system's audio
(`NSMicrophoneUsageDescription`, `NSAudioCaptureUsageDescription`), are
translated as Xcode's projects translate them: by an `InfoPlist.strings`
of the language among the app's [resources](#platform-resources), which
the build keeps, adding the app's name where the file has none.

```
resources/darwin/
├── ja.lproj/InfoPlist.strings        "NSMicrophoneUsageDescription" = "音声メモを録音します。";
└── zh-Hans.lproj/InfoPlist.strings   "NSMicrophoneUsageDescription" = "用麦克风录语音笔记。";
```

The file is the text format Xcode writes, in UTF-8 or UTF-16, or a
property list in XML.

## URL schemes and file types

`urlSchemes` and `fileAssociations` in the configuration (see
[deep links](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/app.md#deep-links) and [file associations](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/app.md#file-associations))
are registered by each package: in the macOS app's `Info.plist`, by the
Windows installer, and by the Linux desktop entry, install script and
Debian package.

## Publishing

With `updates.github` set in the configuration, `mygo build -upload` uploads the
disk images, installers, packages, Linux archives and install script, and
update files to the GitHub release of the version, tagged `v1.2.0`,
creating it as a draft. Review the draft and publish it. It needs the
[GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com) (`gh`), signed in. With `updates.s3`,
it uploads them to a bucket of Amazon S3 or of a compatible service, such
as Cloudflare R2, with the credentials in `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and
`AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` (see [publishing to S3](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md#publishing-to-s3)).

Build on each platform in CI and upload to the same release: macOS runners
sign, notarize and make the disk images; any runner compiles and packages
Windows and Linux apps. Keep the signing secrets in CI secrets:
`MYGO_WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, `MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY`, and the
notary credentials in a keychain of the macOS runner.
[GitHub Actions](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/github-actions.md) has a workflow that does it all.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/documents.md

# Documents

Apps whose windows each show a file, such as a text editor, a drawing app
or a notes app, are document-based apps. `mygo.NewDocuments` gives them
what AppKit's `NSDocument` and SwiftUI's `DocumentGroup` give Mac apps, on
every platform:

* a window per document, with its name in the title, and on macOS the
  file's icon in the title bar and a dot in the close button while it has
  unsaved changes;
* New, Open, Open Recent, Save, Save As, Duplicate, Rename, Move To and
  Revert, in the File menu;
* autosave, and asking to save only where saving can't happen by itself;
* a recovery copy of every unsaved change, so that a crash or a quit loses
  nothing;
* the documents opened from Finder, Explorer, the Dock and the jump list;
* the files that other apps change while they are open.

A notes editor in [native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui.md), the whole app:

```go
func main() {
	mygo.NewDocuments(mygo.DocumentsOptions[string]{
		Types: []mygo.DocumentType{{Name: "Markdown Document", Extensions: []string{"md"}}},
		Read: func(r io.Reader) (string, error) {
			b, err := io.ReadAll(r)
			return string(b), err
		},
		Write: func(w io.Writer, text string) error {
			_, err := io.WriteString(w, text)
			return err
		},
		Equal: func(a, b string) bool { return a == b },
		Window: func(doc *mygo.Document[string]) *mygo.Window {
			text := doc.Content()
			var win *mygo.Window
			win = mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{Content: ui.View(func(c *ui.Context) {
				ui.TextArea(c, &text).Fill().OnChange(func() { doc.Set(text) })
			})})
			doc.OnReload(func() { text = doc.Content(); win.Update(func() {}) })
			return win
		},
	})
	if err := mygo.App.Run(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

`examples/documents` is this editor with a status line and a bar for files
changed by other apps:

```sh
go run ./cmd/mygo dev examples/documents
```

## Documents and their content

`DocumentsOptions[T]` describes one kind of document, whose content is a
`T`:

| field           |                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Types`         | the kinds of files, by name and extensions, e.g. `{Name: "Markdown Document", Extensions: []string{"md", "markdown"}}`. Open dialogs show them; new documents are saved with the first extension |
| `Read`          | reads a content from a file, on a goroutine                                                                                                                                                      |
| `Write`         | writes a content to a file, on a goroutine                                                                                                                                                       |
| `Window`        | creates the window of a document, on the main thread                                                                                                                                             |
| `New`           | the content of a new document; the zero `T` without it                                                                                                                                           |
| `Equal`         | compares contents, so that undoing back to what the file has leaves the document unedited                                                                                                        |
| `Snapshot`      | copies a mutable content before it is written                                                                                                                                                    |
| `Autosave`      | `AutosaveInPlace` (the default) or `AutosaveOff`                                                                                                                                                 |
| `AutosaveDelay` | how long after the last edit an autosave happens: 5 seconds                                                                                                                                      |
| `AskOnQuit`     | asks to save at quit, rather than keeping the documents for the next launch                                                                                                                      |
| `NoUntitled`    | no untitled document when the app starts with nothing to open                                                                                                                                    |

Call `NewDocuments` before `App.Run`. When the app starts, it opens the
files the app was started with, the documents a crash or a quit left with
unsaved changes, or else a new untitled document. An app may make several
kinds of documents; the first is the one File > New creates.

A `Document[T]` is an open document. Its methods are safe from any
goroutine:

```go
doc.Content()   // the content
doc.Set(v)      // replaces it, which edits the document
doc.State()     // name, path, edited, read-only, conflict, deleted
doc.Window()    // its window
doc.Save()      // as File > Save
```

### Values and mutable contents

The content is best a value the app replaces with `Set`: a string, a
struct of values, or a persistent snapshot such as `ui.TextSnapshot` or
`editor.Snapshot`, which share what they don't change. Saving writes the
content as it was when saving started, on a goroutine, while the user goes
on editing, so a value that nothing changes is already a snapshot.

A mutable content, such as a pointer to a model the app changes in place,
gives `Snapshot`, which copies it on the main thread, where the app changes
it, and tells about changes with `Changed`:

```go
mygo.DocumentsOptions[*Drawing]{
	Snapshot: func(d *Drawing) *Drawing { return d.Clone() },
	// …
}

drawing.Shapes = append(drawing.Shapes, shape)
doc.Changed()
```

### The edited state

A document is edited when its content differs from its file's:

* `Set` and `Changed` edit it. With `Equal`, a `Set` of the content the
  file has makes it unedited again, which is what undoing back to it, or
  typing a character and deleting it, does: the undo of text widgets just
  works.
* `SetEdited` sets it, for an app that knows better, such as one keeping
  its own undo history: `false` makes the content what the file has,
  without writing it.
* Saving makes it unedited, unless it changed while it was written: those
  changes stay unsaved.

`OnStateChange` tells about changes of the state, on the main thread.

## Windows

The window of a document shows its name: the file's name, or "Untitled",
"Untitled 2"… in the language the app shows. The title of a document's window is its name on macOS, and
on Linux and Windows the name and the app's, as Notepad and gedit show
them. A page's `<title>` doesn't change it.

While the document has unsaved changes, macOS shows a dot in the window's
close button and Linux and Windows a `*` before the title. On macOS the
title bar also shows the file's icon, which the user drags to another app,
and Command-clicking the title lists the folders the file is in.

Windows of any app can show the same, with `Window.SetRepresentedFile` and
`Window.SetDocumentEdited`. `Window.Title` returns the title without the
`*`.

## Saving

|                |                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Save()`       | writes the document to its file. An untitled document asks where, a read-only one asks for another file, and one whose file another app changed asks whether to overwrite it. `ErrCanceled` tells that the user canceled |
| `SaveAs(path)` | writes it to another file, which the document then is; `""` asks where                                                                                                                                                   |
| `SaveAnyway()` | writes it even when another app changed its file                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `Duplicate()`  | opens an untitled copy, named "Notes copy"                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `Rename(name)` | renames its file, in its folder; `""` asks                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `MoveTo(dir)`  | moves its file to another folder; `""` asks                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `Revert()`     | reads its file again, dropping its unsaved changes                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `Close()`      | closes its window, which asks to save first where it must                                                                                                                                                                |

Files are written as `NSDocument` and GIO write them: into a new file next
to the document, flushed to the disk, which then replaces it, so that a
crash or a full disk never leaves half a file. The file keeps its metadata:
on macOS through `NSFileManager`, which keeps its permissions, creation
date, Finder tags and other extended attributes, ACLs, and its identity, so
aliases still find it; on Windows through `ReplaceFileW`, which keeps its
security descriptor, attributes, alternate data streams and creation time,
and waits a moment for another program holding it open; on Linux with its
permissions, owner and group. A symbolic link's target is replaced, and a
file with other hard links, or in a folder the user can't create files in,
is written in place. When `ReplaceFileW` stops halfway, having removed the
file, the new one is moved into its place; if even that fails, the new file
stays next to where the document was, and the save's error names it.

Before writing, the file is compared with what the document last read or
wrote (its modification time and size): when another app changed it,
`Save` asks, and autosave writes nothing.

## Autosave

With `AutosaveInPlace`, the default, a document is saved to its file a
moment after the user stops editing (`AutosaveDelay`, and at least every
30 seconds while the user keeps editing), when its window loses the focus,
and when it closes, as Mac apps do. Saved documents never ask to be saved.

Documents that can't be saved in place aren't: untitled documents,
documents whose files are read-only, were deleted, or were changed by
another app. Those ask when they close.

With `AutosaveOff`, documents are saved when the user saves them, and ask
when they close, as Windows and Linux apps traditionally do.

## Recovery copies

Every document with unsaved changes that autosave doesn't write keeps a
recovery copy, a second after the user stops editing, as VS Code's backups
and Zed's database keep theirs: an untitled document, a document of an app
without autosave, a document in conflict. The copies are in
`Recovery/<kind>` in `PathUserData`, written by `Write`, with the file's
modification time and size, and go when the document is saved, reverted or
closed without saving.

When the app starts, the documents a crash or a forced quit left come back,
edited. A document whose file changed meanwhile is in conflict. Each
running instance of the app keeps its copies in a session of its own,
locked while it runs, so another instance never opens them.

## Closing and quitting

|                                                                                  | asks                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| closing an unedited document                                                     | nothing                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| closing a saved, edited document, with autosave                                  | nothing: it is saved first                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| closing an edited untitled document, with autosave                               | "Do you want to keep this new document “Untitled”?" Save…, Delete, Cancel                                                                                                                                                                         |
| closing an edited document without autosave, or one that can't be saved in place | "Do you want to save the changes made to the document “Notes.md”?" Save, Don't Save, Cancel                                                                                                                                                       |
| quitting                                                                         | nothing: the documents are saved in place or kept, and come back edited at the next launch                                                                                                                                                        |
| quitting with `AskOnQuit`, several documents                                     | macOS: "You have 3 documents with unsaved changes. Do you want to review these changes before quitting?" Review Changes…, Discard Changes, Cancel, then a sheet for each. Linux and Windows: one dialog naming them, Save All, Don't Save, Cancel |

The questions, their buttons, and the names of untitled documents are
[MyGo's own strings](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/i18n.md#mygos-own-strings), in the language the app
shows. On macOS the questions are sheets of the document's window. A close that
must ask keeps the window open until the user answers; a quit waits for the
documents, then quits, and Cancel keeps every window open. The quit's
`OnBeforeQuit` listeners run again then.

A window destroyed without asking (`Window.Destroy`, `App.Exit`) keeps the
recovery copy of its document's unsaved changes, which come back at the
next launch.

## Files changed by other apps

Documents watch their files (see [watching
files](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md#watching-files)), and look at their file when their window
is focused, as VS Code and Notepad++ do, since watches miss changes:

* a document without unsaved changes reads its file again, and
  `OnReload` tells the app to show the new content;
* a document with unsaved changes is in conflict: its state says so, and
  saving asks whether to keep it or the other app's ("Save Anyway",
  "Revert");
* a file renamed by another app, in its folder, is followed;
* a deleted file leaves its document open, `Deleted` in its state, and
  saving writes the file again.

## The File menu

The menu roles of documents act on the document of the focused window, and
are enabled for it:

| role             | macOS           | Linux, Windows        |
| ---------------- | --------------- | --------------------- |
| `RoleNew`        | New ⌘N          | New Ctrl+N            |
| `RoleOpen`       | Open… ⌘O        | Open… Ctrl+O          |
| `RoleOpenRecent` | Open Recent     | Open Recent           |
| `RoleSave`       | Save ⌘S         | Save Ctrl+S           |
| `RoleSaveAs`     | Save As… ⌥⇧⌘S   | Save As… Ctrl+Shift+S |
| `RoleDuplicate`  | Duplicate ⇧⌘S   | Duplicate             |
| `RoleRename`     | Rename…         | Rename…               |
| `RoleMoveTo`     | Move To…        | Move To…              |
| `RoleRevert`     | Revert to Saved | Revert                |

`RoleFileMenu` holds the File menu of each platform when the app has
documents: DocumentGroup's on macOS (New, Open, Open Recent, Close, Save,
Duplicate, Rename, Move To, Revert to Saved), Notepad's and KDE's
elsewhere (New, Open, Open Recent, Save, Save As, Revert, Close, Quit).
Apps with documents get a menu bar on Linux and Windows too, with File and
Edit menus, until they set their own.

Open Recent lists the documents the app opened and saved lately, newest
first, which `App.RecentDocuments` returns: documents record their files
with `App.AddRecentDocument`, which also records them with the system (the
Dock menu on macOS, the jump list on Windows, the recently used files on
Linux), and its Clear Menu calls `App.ClearRecentDocuments`. See
[recent documents](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/app.md#recent-documents).

## Opening files

Documents open the files the system asks the app to open (`App.OnOpenFile`)
of their extensions: from Finder or Explorer, the Dock or the jump list, or
the command line. List the types in `fileAssociations` of the
[configuration](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md), which makes the system offer the app
for them:

```json
"fileAssociations": [
  { "ext": ["md", "markdown"], "name": "Markdown Document", "mimeType": "text/markdown" }
]
```

On Linux and Windows every file opened starts the app again: call
`App.RequestSingleInstanceLock` so that the first instance opens them.

A file that is open already focuses its window. On macOS the app stays open
without windows, as document apps do, and clicking its Dock icon makes an
untitled document.

## Web pages

The pages of document windows get their documents through the generated
TypeScript client: bind the service of the documents under the name the
client calls it by,

```go
notes := mygo.NewDocuments(mygo.DocumentsOptions[Note]{ /* … */ })
mygo.BindAs("Note", notes.Service())
```

and the page reads and replaces the content of its window's document, and
follows its state:

```ts
import { Note } from "./mygo"; // generated
import { onDocumentReload, onDocumentState } from "mygo-runtime";

editor.value = (await Note.content()).body;
editor.oninput = () => Note.setContent({ body: editor.value });
onDocumentState(({ name, edited }) => { status.textContent = edited ? "Edited" : "Saved" });
onDocumentReload(async () => { editor.value = (await Note.content()).body });
```

The service has `content`, `setContent`, `state`, `save`, `saveAs`,
`duplicate`, `rename`, `moveTo` and `revert`, for the window that calls
them. A page sending its whole content on every keystroke suits notes and
small documents; for large ones, send it when the user pauses.

## Platform differences

|                       | macOS                                              | Linux                              | Windows              |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| edited mark           | dot in the close button                            | `*` before the title               | `*` before the title |
| file in the title bar | proxy icon, Command-click for its folders          | none                               | none                 |
| title                 | the name                                           | name - app                         | name - app           |
| replacing files       | `NSFileManager` `replaceItemAtURL:`                | rename, with mode, owner and group | `ReplaceFileW`       |
| questions             | sheets of the window                               | dialogs                            | dialogs              |
| without windows       | the app stays open; the Dock icon makes a document | the app quits                      | the app quits        |

## What is left out

What only a real `NSDocument` does on macOS: renaming in the title bar's
popover, "— Edited" next to the title, browsing versions and Revert To a
version, locking files, and drafts in iCloud. Documents that are folders
(packages) aren't supported yet, and browsers have no files to open.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/frontend.md

# The frontend

Windows that show web pages show the pages of the app's frontend: HTML,
CSS and JavaScript built with any tools. New projects use TypeScript and
[Vite](https://vite.dev), but MyGo only needs a URL to load, during
development, and a directory of built files, for builds. Windows of
[native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui.md) need no frontend, and an app that only has those has
none.

## How pages load

Windows load pages of the frontend with URLs without a scheme, such as `/`
or `/settings?tab=general`:

```go
mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{URL: "/"})
win.Page().LoadURL("/settings")
```

They resolve against:

* during `mygo dev`, the dev server at `devUrl` in mygo.config.ts, which
  `devCommand` starts, e.g. `http://localhost:5173/`, so the dev server's
  hot reload works in the app;
* in builds, `mygo://localhost/`, which serves the files of `frontendDist`
  that `mygo build` embeds into the executable after running
  `buildCommand`.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  devUrl: "http://localhost:5173",
  devCommand: "bun run dev:web",
  buildCommand: "bun run build:web",
  frontendDist: "dist",
});
```

Without `devUrl`, `mygo dev` serves `frontendDist` from disk instead. Paths
without a file extension that match no file serve `index.html`, so
client-side routers work.

The frontend is a secure context, and its origin is `mygo://localhost` on
macOS and Linux and `http://mygo.localhost` on Windows, where WebView2
serves custom schemes under `http://<scheme>.localhost`. Storage such as
`localStorage` and IndexedDB belongs to an origin, so data a page stores
under `mygo dev` (the dev server's origin) is not what the built app sees.
Keep data you care about in Go, for example in a file in
`App.Path(mygo.PathUserData)`, and hand it to pages through bound methods.

Windows can also load other content into their page:

* `win.Page().LoadURL("https://example.com")`, a web page;
* `win.Page().LoadHTML(html, baseURL)`, an HTML string, which reloads load
  again;
* `win.Page().LoadFile("docs/index.html")`, a local file, resolved against the
  working directory, then the executable's directory (and the Resources
  directory of a macOS app).

Pages that are not the app's own cannot call Go methods: see
[who may call](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/bindings.md#who-may-call).

### Without the CLI

`mygo build` embeds the frontend by calling `mygo.SetFrontend`, and a
program built with `go build` can do the same with `embed`:

```go
//go:embed all:dist
var dist embed.FS

func main() {
	web, _ := fs.Sub(dist, "dist")
	mygo.SetFrontend(web)
	// ...
}
```

## Custom protocols

`mygo.Protocol.Handle` serves a URL scheme from an `http.Handler`, for
content your app produces or reads at run time: pages, images, files of
the user. Handlers run on their own goroutines and stream their responses:
writes wait while the webview is behind, so a large file is never held in
memory whole. Pages load such URLs like web URLs, with `fetch`, `<img>`,
ES modules and relative URLs:

```go
// Thumbnails generated into the cache directory.
cache, _ := mygo.App.Path(mygo.PathCache)
mygo.Protocol.Handle("thumbs", mygo.FileServer(os.DirFS(cache)))

// Anything an http.Handler does.
mygo.Protocol.HandleFunc("api", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"path": r.URL.Path})
})
```

```html
<img src="thumbs://localhost/photo-42.png" />
```

Register schemes before creating the windows that use them.
`mygo.FileServer` serves an `fs.FS` with content types and range requests,
falling back to `index.html` like the frontend. Handling the `mygo` scheme
replaces the frontend with your handler. Pages of custom schemes are the
app's own: they may call Go methods, see [trust](#trust).

Audio and video are the exception: WebKitGTK's media player does not play
from a custom scheme, so on Linux a `<video>` or `<audio>` of one fails with
`MEDIA_ERR_SRC_NOT_SUPPORTED` (`error.code` 4), whatever the handler
answers. Serve media from a loopback HTTP server instead, the same on every
platform, and give the page its URL:

```go
ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0") // a free port
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
go http.Serve(ln, mygo.FileServer(os.DirFS(videos)))
mediaURL := "http://" + ln.Addr().String() + "/" // <video src="{mediaURL}clip.mp4">
```

Every program of the machine can reach such a server: serve it only what
they may read, or put a secret of the app's in its paths.

Each scheme is its own origin, so a page fetching another scheme makes a
cross-origin request: the frontend reading `api://localhost/`, or, during
`mygo dev`, the dev server reading `thumbs://localhost/`. Responses to the
app's own pages, those that may call Go methods, carry the CORS headers
that let them read the response, and MyGo answers their preflights.
Other sites get none, unless the window trusts them
(`PageOptions.TrustedOrigins`), and handlers may set their own.
On Windows, fetch a scheme at `http://<scheme>.localhost/`, where
WebView2 serves it, and another host at `http://<host>.<scheme>.localhost/`
(`myapp://abc/` is `http://abc.myapp.localhost/`). Such hosts are DNS
names (letters, digits, hyphens and dots) and are reported in lower case;
URLs with another host or a port aren't served there.

### Trust

A window trusts the app's own pages: its frontend, pages of custom schemes,
`file:` and `about:` pages (`LoadHTML` without a base URL shows
`about:blank`), origins in `PageOptions.TrustedOrigins`, and in development
builds pages served from localhost. Trust follows the page's URL, in a
window or a [web view](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/web-view.md), and changes as it navigates. A
trusted page may:

* call every method bound with `mygo.Bind`, and the plugins the app uses;
* call `window.mygo.window` to set the title of its window, minimize,
  maximize, full-screen or close it;
* get the camera, the microphone, the location and notifications without a
  permission handler;
* read the responses of every custom scheme, which carry CORS headers for
  it;
* hear the paths of the files dropped on it, and of its window's document.

So never serve third-party or user-supplied HTML from a custom scheme, nor
load it with `LoadHTML` without a base URL: a plugin's UI or a preview of
a user's HTML would get all of the above. Show it from an origin the
window does not trust instead, such as an `https` site or a `data:` URL:
it calls no Go method, and gets no permission unless a
[permission handler](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#permissions) grants it.

Some things reach every page, trusted or not:

* events: `Broadcast` sends to every page of every window, and `Emit` to
  every web view of a window of native UI. Send to one page with
  `EmitPage`.
* messages to Go: an untrusted page's calls are rejected, but the app
  receives and decodes them first, whatever their size.
* `window.open` and `target="_blank"` links open `http(s)` URLs in the
  default browser, unless `SetWindowOpenHandler` decides
  ([links and new windows](#links-and-new-windows)).
* downloads go to the Downloads directory, unless `OnWillDownload` decides
  ([downloads](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#downloads)).
* the page may navigate anywhere, unless `OnWillNavigate` cancels it
  ([pages](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#pages)). A page that navigates to a trusted URL is
  trusted.

## The mygo-runtime package

MyGo injects its runtime into every page as `window.mygo`. The
`mygo-runtime` npm package, which new projects depend on, gives it types
and imports; the generated client is built on it.

```ts
import { currentWindow, isMyGo, onFileDrop, runtime } from "mygo-runtime";

if (isMyGo() && runtime().platform === "darwin") {
  document.documentElement.classList.add("mac");
}

await currentWindow.toggleMaximize();
```

| Export                                                                                    | What it does                                                                                                                                                                               |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `call(method, ...args)`, `on(event, listener)`, `once(event, listener)`, `event<T>(name)` | untyped calls and events, see [bindings](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/bindings.md#without-the-generated-client)                                                                            |
| `Channel`                                                                                 | a stream of values from a Go method, see [channels](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/bindings.md#channels)                                                                                     |
| `isCallError(err)`                                                                        | whether a rejection came from a Go error                                                                                                                                                   |
| `isMyGo()`                                                                                | whether the page runs in a MyGo window, not in a browser tab of the dev server                                                                                                             |
| `runtime()`                                                                               | the runtime: `platform` (`"darwin"`, `"linux"` or `"win32"`), `windowId` (the Go window's `ID()`) and `version`; throws outside MyGo                                                       |
| `currentWindow`                                                                           | the page's window: `minimize`, `maximize`, `unmaximize`, `toggleMaximize`, `isMaximized`, `toggleFullScreen`, `close` and `setTitle`                                                       |
| `onFileDrop(listener)`                                                                    | files dropped on the window, with their paths                                                                                                                                              |
| `preferences()`                                                                           | the accent color and the accessibility settings of the desktop; throws outside MyGo                                                                                                        |
| `onPreferences(listener)`                                                                 | the changes of `preferences()`                                                                                                                                                             |
| `locale()`, `direction()`, `onLocaleChange(listener)`                                     | the language the app shows (`App.Locale`), such as `"zh-Hans"`, its direction, `"ltr"` or `"rtl"`, and its changes; the page has them from document start, as `mygo.locale` and `mygo.dir` |

`mygo-runtime/i18n` formats messages of ICU MessageFormat, as package
`i18n` does in Go. The module `mygo generate` writes for the app's
[catalogs](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/i18n.md#in-pages), `locales.ts`, is built on it, and holds the
messages of every language, which the frontend's build bundles: a page
says its first words in the app's language without waiting for a request.

Opened in a regular browser, which is handy for working on the layout,
pages have no runtime: calls reject and `isMyGo()` is false.

## Custom title bars

A frameless window has no title bar or borders, and the page draws its own.
Mark the elements that drag the window with the CSS property
`--app-region: drag`:

```go
mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{URL: "/", Frameless: true})
```

```css
.titlebar {
  --app-region: drag;
  height: 40px;
}
.titlebar .search {
  --app-region: no-drag;
}
```

```ts
import { currentWindow } from "mygo-runtime";

minimizeButton.onclick = () => currentWindow.minimize();
maximizeButton.onclick = () => currentWindow.toggleMaximize();
closeButton.onclick = () => currentWindow.close();
```

The property is inherited: `no-drag` excludes parts of a region again, and
buttons, links, inputs and other interactive elements inside a region stay
clickable. Double-clicking a region does what double-clicking a title bar
does.

Frameless windows still resize from their edges. On Linux under Wayland,
GTK decorates frameless windows and windows with a hidden title bar itself,
as GNOME's apps, without a title bar: it draws a shadow and a thin border
around the page, which resize the window from just outside it, and drops
them while the window is maximized or in full screen. Elsewhere on Linux,
where GTK gives windows without decorations no borders (X11, or a window
with `DisableShadow`, `Transparent` or `Panel`), the outermost 5 px of the
page act as the borders: they show resize cursors, and the page gets no
clicks or pointer moves there.

On Linux a frameless window also keeps the menu bar that `App.SetMenu` or
`Window.SetMenu` gives it, above the page and so above a custom title bar.
Give such a window an empty menu of its own,
`win.SetMenu(mygo.NewMenu(nil))`, and show menus from the page instead
(`Menu.PopupAt`, from a bound method the page calls).

### Hidden title bars

A window can keep its window controls and only hide the title bar, so the
page extends under them and draws the rest of the title bar: set
`TitleBarStyle` to `mygo.TitleBarHidden`. The controls stay at the top of
the window:

* On macOS, the traffic lights. `mygo.TitleBarHiddenInset` leaves more
  room around them, and `TrafficLightPosition` moves them: the position of
  the close button's top-left corner in the window.
* On Windows, minimize, maximize or restore, and close at the top-right
  corner, drawn as Windows 11 draws its own. They fill the height of the
  title bar, `TitleBarHeight` (32 by default), and hovering maximize opens
  the snap layouts. The window resizes from its top edge.
* On Linux, GTK's own title buttons, where the desktop's button layout puts
  them, centered in `TitleBarHeight` (by default the height of the
  desktop's header bars). The layout decides which buttons show, possibly
  none, as tiling window managers are often set up. A Wayland compositor
  that decorates windows itself, as KWin, Hyprland and Sway do, has none:
  its own title bar holds the buttons, and a tiling one shows none. The
  outer pixels of the page resize the window, as a frameless one's. The
  window's menu bar hides, as with `AutoHideMenuBar`: Alt and F10 show it
  above the page while its menus are open, and its shortcuts work all
  along.

```go
mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{
	URL:            "/",
	TitleBarStyle:  mygo.TitleBarHidden,
	TitleBarHeight: 40,
})
```

From its first paint, the page learns the room the controls take from
CSS variables on `:root`:

| variable                                                    |                                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--mygo-titlebar-height`                                    | the height of the title bar                                      |
| `--mygo-titlebar-inset-left`, `--mygo-titlebar-inset-right` | the room the controls take from the left and from the right edge |

They are `0px` in full screen, where the controls hide (on macOS they come
back with the menu bar). The page's title bar keeps clear of the controls
and, marked with `--app-region: drag`, moves the window:

```css
.titlebar {
  --app-region: drag;
  height: var(--mygo-titlebar-height, 40px);
  padding-left: var(--mygo-titlebar-inset-left, 0px);
  padding-right: var(--mygo-titlebar-inset-right, 0px);
}
```

`Transparent: true` lets a page with a transparent background show the
desktop through, and `Vibrancy` puts a blurred material behind it on macOS
and Windows 11 22H2 and later:

```go
mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{
	URL:           "/",
	TitleBarStyle: mygo.TitleBarHidden,
	Transparent:   true,
	Vibrancy:      mygo.VibrancySidebar, // Mica on Windows 11
})
```

See `examples/frameless` for a complete custom title bar. Native UI shows
materials the same way ([Vibrancy](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/windows.md#vibrancy)), as
`examples/vibrancy` does in a translucent sidebar under an inset title bar.

## Dropped files

Files dragged from Finder or Explorer and dropped on the page reach the
page with their paths, which DOM drop events do not tell:

```ts
import { onFileDrop } from "mygo-runtime";

onFileDrop(({ paths, x, y }) => {
  const target = document.elementFromPoint(x, y);
  // ...
});
```

and Go, with `win.OnFileDrop`. The page's own drag and drop keeps working:
its drop listeners still get the `File` objects, and dropping files where
the page does not handle them no longer replaces the page with the file.

## Dark mode

Pages follow the system appearance through the `prefers-color-scheme` media
query. Declare `color-scheme: light dark` in CSS so that form controls and
scrollbars follow too, and give windows a `BackgroundColor` matching the
page in both appearances, which the window shows until the page paints:

```css
:root {
  color-scheme: light dark;
}
```

```go
mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{URL: "/", BackgroundColor: "light-dark(#f5f5f7, #1e1e1e)"})
```

`mygo.Theme.SetSource(mygo.ThemeDark)` forces an appearance, which pages see
through the same media query.

## Accent color and accessibility

`prefers-reduced-motion` and `prefers-contrast` follow the desktop on their
own. The accent color the desktop uses and the factor it asks text to grow
by are what the media queries do not tell a page: they are CSS variables on
`:root` from the first paint.

| variable            |                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--mygo-accent`     | the accent as `#rrggbb`; unset where the desktop has none, so `var(--mygo-accent, AccentColor)` falls back to the desktop's own color |
| `--mygo-text-scale` | the factor text grows by; `1` is the usual size, so `calc(1rem * var(--mygo-text-scale, 1))`                                          |

```css
:root {
  --accent: var(--mygo-accent, AccentColor);
  font-size: calc(1rem * var(--mygo-text-scale, 1));
}
```

`preferences()` of `mygo-runtime` returns the settings themselves, current
from document start on, and `onPreferences` tells their changes, which only
the desktop makes; a component reads the first and subscribes to the
second, as with `matchMedia`:

```ts
import { onPreferences, preferences, type ThemePreferences } from "mygo-runtime";

const apply = ({ reduceTransparency }: ThemePreferences) =>
  document.documentElement.classList.toggle("opaque", reduceTransparency);
apply(preferences());
const off = onPreferences(apply);
```

| field                |                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `accent`             | the accent as `"#rrggbb"`, or `null` where the desktop has none                                                                                         |
| `reduceMotion`       | the desktop asks for less motion, as `prefers-reduced-motion`                                                                                           |
| `reduceTransparency` | the desktop asks for opaque surfaces: macOS's Reduce Transparency, Windows's transparency effects turned off; false on Linux, which has no such setting |
| `highContrast`       | the desktop asks for more contrast, as `prefers-contrast: more`                                                                                         |
| `textScale`          | how many times larger than usual text should be; `1` is usual                                                                                           |

A page that navigates starts with the values of the moment: the script
that tells them at document start is replaced when they change.
`mygo.Theme.Preferences()` reads them on the Go side, see
[native](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md#accent-color-and-accessibility).

## Pages that size their window

The page of a flyout or a window with `FitContent` sizes it, without a
`ResizeObserver` or a bound method of its own: MyGo's runtime lays `html`
out at the width of its content, within the window's limits, and the
window takes the root's size as it changes (see
[windows](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#size-a-flyout-to-its-content)). Let `html` and
`body` take their content's size: a `height: 100%` or `100vh` on them
keeps the window at the size it has, and a `width` on `html` replaces the
content's. Text wider than the maximum wraps, and content taller than it
scrolls.

## Links and new windows

Links with `target="_blank"` and `window.open()` call the window's open
handler. Without one, `http(s)` URLs open in the default browser and
anything else is denied; `win.Page().SetWindowOpenHandler` decides otherwise:

```go
win.Page().SetWindowOpenHandler(func(req mygo.WindowOpenRequest) *mygo.WindowOptions {
	if strings.HasPrefix(req.URL, "https://docs.example.com/") {
		return &mygo.WindowOptions{Width: 900, Height: 700} // a window of the app
	}
	go mygo.Shell.OpenExternal(req.URL) // the default browser
	return nil
})
```

`req.UserInitiated` tells the windows a user opened, with a click on the link
or a click or key press whose handler calls `window.open()`, from the ones a
script opened on its own, as a pop-up from a timer or as the page loads.
Refuse those, as ads in an embedded page:

```go
win.Page().SetWindowOpenHandler(func(req mygo.WindowOpenRequest) *mygo.WindowOptions {
	if !req.UserInitiated {
		return nil // a pop-up
	}
	go mygo.Shell.OpenExternal(req.URL)
	return nil
})
```

On Linux, WebKitGTK blocks a `window.open()` without a user's gesture itself,
so the handler is asked only about the ones a gesture made. A script the app
runs itself with `Page.Eval` counts as a user's gesture on macOS and Linux,
where WebKit runs it as one.

`win.Page().OnWillNavigate` can cancel the page's own navigations, e.g. to keep the
app's window on the app: see [Windows](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#pages).

## Preload scripts

`PageOptions.PreloadScript` runs JavaScript in every page of the window
before the page's own scripts, once `window.mygo` exists.

## The web inspector

Development builds have the web inspector: right-click a page and choose
Inspect Element (Inspect on Windows), or call `win.Page().OpenDevTools()`.
Production builds do not, unless built with `mygo build -debug` or a window's
page sets `DevTools: mygo.DevToolsEnabled` in `WindowOptions.Page`.

On Windows, WebView2's own keys come with the inspector: F5 and Ctrl+R reload
the page (a reload [`OnWillNavigate`](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#pages) is not asked about),
Ctrl+P prints, Ctrl+F finds and Ctrl+Plus zooms only where the inspector is
on. Without it, as in production builds, a page has none of them, as on macOS
and Linux, and only the app's menu items take these keys, such as the View
menu's (`RoleViewMenu`).
