Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/getting-started.md

# Getting started

A MyGo app shows its windows with a web frontend, in the system's webview,
or with [native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui.md) that MyGo draws itself, written in Go. `mygo
init` starts a project of either kind, and an app can add windows of the
other kind later.

## Install

Install [Go](https://go.dev/dl/) 1.27 or later. A project with a web
frontend also needs [Bun](https://bun.sh), which runs its tools, and apps
with web pages need the system's webview:

* on Linux, GTK 3 and WebKitGTK 4.1, e.g.
  `sudo apt install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0` on Debian and Ubuntu;
* on Windows 10, the
  [WebView2 Runtime](https://developer.microsoft.com/microsoft-edge/webview2/),
  which Windows 11 includes.

Native UI needs nothing more: Go builds the app, and it runs on what the
system has (GTK 3 on Linux).

The `mygo` command line tool creates, runs and packages apps. It is a Go
program, which Go runs without installing it:

```sh
go run github.com/egoist/mygo/cmd/mygo@latest init my-app
```

Projects with a web frontend also depend on it through npm, as the
`mygo-cli` package, so Bun or npm create one too:

```sh
bunx mygo-cli init my-app      # or: npx mygo-cli init my-app
```

You can also install the CLI with Go, which puts `mygo` on your `PATH`:

```sh
go install github.com/egoist/mygo/cmd/mygo@latest
mygo init my-app
```

`mygo doctor` checks that the machine has what MyGo needs.

## Create a project

### A web frontend

`mygo init my-app` creates a Go module and a TypeScript frontend built with
[Vite](https://vite.dev), side by side, and installs their dependencies:

```
my-app/
├── main.go          the app: its windows and the Go code the page calls
├── go.mod
├── mygo.config.ts   the app's name, identifier and version, and how to build it
├── package.json     the scripts, and the frontend's dependencies
├── index.html       the page
├── src/
│   ├── main.ts      the page's code
│   ├── style.css
│   └── mygo.ts      the typed client of the Go code, generated
├── vite.config.ts
├── tsconfig.json
└── resources/
    └── icon.png     the app icon, a 1024×1024 PNG
```

Builds go to `dist/` (the frontend) and `build/` (the packaged apps), and
the development app to `.mygo/`; `.gitignore` leaves them out. See
[configuration](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md) for the fields of `mygo.config.ts`.

### Native UI

`mygo init -template native my-app` creates an app whose window shows
[native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui.md): a Go module alone, with no frontend and no Bun.

```
my-app/
├── main.go          the app: its state, its view and its window
├── main_test.go     a test of the view, which runs without a window
├── go.mod           with the CLI as a tool
├── mygo.json        the app's name, identifier and version
└── resources/
    └── icon.png     the app icon, a 1024×1024 PNG
```

The module has the CLI as a
[tool](https://go.dev/doc/modules/managing-dependencies#tools): `go tool
mygo` runs it at the version `go.mod` pins, which
`go get -tool github.com/egoist/mygo/cmd/mygo@latest` updates with MyGo.

## Develop

```sh
cd my-app
bun run dev        # a web frontend: runs mygo dev
go tool mygo dev   # native UI
```

`mygo dev` builds a development version of the app and starts it, then
rebuilds and restarts it when you edit a `.go` file, the configuration, the
icon or a resource. A build that fails to compile keeps the previous one
running. Quit the app, or press Ctrl+C, to stop.

With a web frontend, it also writes `src/mygo.ts` and starts the Vite dev
server, from which the development app loads its pages: edit `src/main.ts`
or `src/style.css` and Vite updates the page right away. Development builds
have the web inspector: right-click the page and choose Inspect Element
(Inspect on Windows), or call `win.Page().OpenDevTools()`.

On macOS the development app is a real app bundle, `My App Dev` with the
identifier of the app plus `.dev`, so that it keeps its data, preferences
and permissions apart from the installed app.

## Call Go

### From the page

`main.go` binds a Go value, whose exported methods the page can call:

```go
// Greeter is callable from the frontend: `mygo generate` turns its methods
// into typed TypeScript functions in src/mygo.ts.
type Greeter struct{}

// Greet returns a greeting for name.
func (Greeter) Greet(name string) string {
	if name == "" {
		name = "stranger"
	}
	return "Hello, " + name + "! This message comes from Go."
}

// Tick is sent to the page every second.
var Tick = mygo.NewEvent[time.Time]("tick")

func main() {
	mygo.Bind(Greeter{})
	// ...
}
```

`src/mygo.ts`, which mygo dev keeps up to date, turns them into typed
functions and events:

```ts
import { Greeter, events } from "./mygo";

const greeting = await Greeter.greet("Ada"); // Promise<string>
events.tick.on((time) => console.log(time)); // time: string
```

Add a method to `Greeter`, save, and it is there to call once the app has
restarted. [Calling Go from the frontend](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/bindings.md) covers what methods
can take and return, errors, events and security.

### From native UI

Native UI is Go, so it calls your code directly, with no bindings. The view
is a function of your app's state that MyGo calls to build each frame; it
asks its elements what happened since the last one:

```go
func (a *app) view(c *ui.Context) {
	ui.Column(c).Fill().Center().Gap(16).Children(func() {
		ui.TextInput(c, &a.name).Placeholder("Your name").Width(240)
		if ui.PrimaryButton(c, "Greet").Clicked() {
			a.greeting = greet(a.name) // your Go code
		}
		ui.Text(c, a.greeting)
	})
}
```

`main_test.go` clicks and types into the view without a window, as fast as
a unit test: run `go test`. [Native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui.md) covers layout, widgets,
text, input, drawing and changing the state from other goroutines.

## Build

```sh
bun run build        # a web frontend: runs mygo build
go tool mygo build   # native UI
```

`mygo build` compiles the app, with the frontend built by Vite embedded in
it when there is one, and packages it for the machine's platform in
`build/<os>-<arch>/`:

| Platform | Output                                                                                                                                         |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| macOS    | `My App.app`, and a disk image `my-app-0.1.0-arm64.dmg`                                                                                        |
| Windows  | `My App.exe`, and an installer `my-app-setup-0.1.0-amd64.exe`                                                                                  |
| Linux    | the executable `my-app` with its desktop entry and icon, their archive with `install.sh`, which installs it for the user, and a `.deb` package |

MyGo needs no cgo, so any machine builds for every platform:

```sh
bun run build -- -platform darwin/universal,windows/amd64,linux/amd64
go tool mygo build -platform darwin/universal,windows/amd64,linux/amd64
```

The apps run where they are, but to ship them to users, sign them: see
[Building and distributing](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/distribution.md).

## Next steps

* [Windows](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md) and [the application](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/app.md), to shape the app.
* [Native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui.md), to build interfaces in Go, or
  [the frontend](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/frontend.md), for web pages.
* [Menus and the tray](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/menus.md) and the [desktop APIs](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md).
* The examples in the repository:
  * with web pages: `examples/hello` (the smallest app), `examples/todo`
    (typed services and events, persistence, dialogs, menus, several
    windows), `examples/frameless` (a custom title bar) and
    `examples/native` (menus, a tray icon, dialogs, notifications, a
    global shortcut, the clipboard and dark mode);
  * with native UI: `examples/clipboard` (copying and dragging text, HTML,
    lazy JSON, and file lists), `examples/counter-native` (a counter with a test of its
    view), `examples/vibrancy` (a translucent sidebar under an inset title
    bar, its material picked in it), `examples/effort-slider` (a web
    demo's animated slider redrawn: letters blurring in, a burst of
    pixels, a shaking card), `examples/confetti` (canvas-confetti's
    demos, every piece flying on poses that only paint), `examples/wind`
    (the glyph texture behind the Claude app's Code tab: characters lit by
    a passing wind, ripples from clicks, drawn by two shaders written in
    Go), `examples/blackhole` (a black hole whose light a shader traces
    through its gravity: the lensed accretion disk, Doppler beaming and an
    Einstein ring of stars, in three passes with bloom), `examples/chat-glow`
    (an assistant lit as Apple Intelligence: the window's edges glowing
    while it thinks, borders of conic gradients blurred, and a glowing
    field, shimmering text and an orb, shaders), `examples/timeline`
    (an intro on one playhead: a card sliding in, its title and rows
    following it, with play, pause, reverse and restart) and
    `examples/gallery` (a tour of the
    toolkit: layout, widgets, text editing, a list of ten thousand rows,
    drawing and overlays).

# GitHub Actions

A GitHub Actions workflow can build the apps of every platform when you
push a tag, sign them, and upload them with their [updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md) to
a draft release, which you publish. Each platform builds on a runner of
its own, at the same time. MyGo needs no cgo, so Ubuntu runners make the
Windows apps as well as the Linux ones; the macOS app needs a macOS runner,
because signing, notarization and disk images need macOS.

## The workflow

With `updates.github` in the configuration, save this as
`.github/workflows/release.yml`:

```yaml
name: Release

on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

permissions:
  contents: write # the draft release, and the uploads to it

jobs:
  draft-release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Create the draft release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          if ! gh release view "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            gh release create "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" \
              --draft --verify-tag --title "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --generate-notes
          fi

  build:
    needs: draft-release
    name: ${{ matrix.name }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        include:
          - { name: macOS, os: macos-latest, platform: "darwin/arm64,darwin/amd64" }
          - { name: Windows, os: ubuntu-latest, platform: "windows/amd64,windows/arm64" }
          - { name: Linux, os: ubuntu-latest, platform: "linux/amd64,linux/arm64" }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v7
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
      - uses: oven-sh/setup-bun@v2
      - run: bun install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Install NSIS, for the Windows installers
        if: matrix.name == 'Windows' && runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y nsis
      - name: Build and upload
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: bun run build -- -platform "${{ matrix.platform }}" -upload
```

A project of [native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui.md) has no frontend, so no Bun: leave out the
`setup-bun` and `bun install` steps, and build with the CLI that `go.mod`
pins as a tool:

```yaml
        run: go tool mygo build -platform "${{ matrix.platform }}" -upload
```

Add the secret key that signs updates, the contents of `mygo-update.key`
(see [auto-updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md#set-up)), to the repository's secrets:

```sh
gh secret set MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY < path/to/mygo-update.key
```

Then bump `version` in the configuration, commit, and push its tag:

```sh
git tag v1.2.0
git push origin v1.2.0
```

The draft release job creates the draft release `v1.2.0`. Then the build
job runs once for each row of its matrix, at the same time, and each
uploads to the draft: the macOS disk images, the Windows installers, and
the Linux archives, Debian packages and install script, each with their
updates.
Review the draft and publish it: apps then update to it.

* `mygo build` uploads to the release of the configuration's version, with
  the `tagPrefix` of `updates` (`v` by default), whichever tag started the
  workflow. A step can check that they agree, as [below](#checking-the-version).
* The draft exists before the builds start, so they upload to it: without
  it, each `mygo build -upload` would create a draft of its own. Running
  the workflow again keeps the draft, and replaces its files.
* With `fail-fast: false`, the other platforms finish when one fails. "Re-run
  failed jobs" builds that one again, and it uploads to the same draft.
* A row's `platform` may list several targets, which `mygo build` builds
  one after the other. A row for each target, such as `windows/amd64` and
  `windows/arm64`, builds them at the same time, on more runners.
* The release page gets the notes that GitHub generates from the pull
  requests since the last release, which you can edit in the draft. The
  update window shows the version's section of `CHANGELOG.md`, which the
  update manifests carry.
* The `GITHUB_TOKEN` of the workflow lets `gh`, which the runners have,
  create the release and upload to it. With a `tagPrefix`, it also lets
  `mygo build` find the earlier releases that
  [delta updates](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md#delta-updates) start from.

As it is, the workflow makes apps that work but are not signed for other
machines: macOS apps signed ad hoc, which Gatekeeper blocks on other Macs,
and Windows apps without a signature, for which SmartScreen warns users.
The next sections sign them.

## Signing and notarizing macOS apps

The macOS row needs your Developer ID certificate and the credentials of
Apple's notary service (see [signing and notarization](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/distribution.md#signing-and-notarization)).
Export the "Developer ID Application" certificate, with its private key,
from Keychain Access as a `.p12` file with a password, and add the
secrets:

```sh
base64 -i certificate.p12 | gh secret set MACOS_CERTIFICATE
gh secret set MACOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD   # the password of the .p12
gh secret set APPLE_ID                     # the Apple ID of your developer account
gh secret set APPLE_TEAM_ID                # your team ID, as in the identity's (TEAMID)
gh secret set APPLE_APP_PASSWORD           # an app-specific password of the Apple ID
```

Create the app-specific password at
[account.apple.com](https://account.apple.com), under Sign-In and Security.
Then, before "Build and upload", put them in a keychain of the macOS
runner:

```yaml
      - name: Import the certificate and the notary credentials
        if: runner.os == 'macOS'
        env:
          MACOS_CERTIFICATE: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERTIFICATE }}
          MACOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.MACOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD }}
          APPLE_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_ID }}
          APPLE_TEAM_ID: ${{ secrets.APPLE_TEAM_ID }}
          APPLE_APP_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.APPLE_APP_PASSWORD }}
        run: |
          keychain="$RUNNER_TEMP/signing.keychain-db"
          password="$(openssl rand -base64 24)"
          security create-keychain -p "$password" "$keychain"
          security set-keychain-settings -lut 21600 "$keychain"
          security unlock-keychain -p "$password" "$keychain"
          echo "$MACOS_CERTIFICATE" | base64 --decode > "$RUNNER_TEMP/certificate.p12"
          security import "$RUNNER_TEMP/certificate.p12" -k "$keychain" \
            -P "$MACOS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD" -T /usr/bin/codesign
          rm "$RUNNER_TEMP/certificate.p12"
          security set-key-partition-list -S apple-tool:,apple: -s -k "$password" "$keychain"
          security list-keychains -d user -s "$keychain" login.keychain
          xcrun notarytool store-credentials notary --keychain "$keychain" \
            --apple-id "$APPLE_ID" --team-id "$APPLE_TEAM_ID" --password "$APPLE_APP_PASSWORD"
          echo "NOTARY_KEYCHAIN=$keychain" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
```

The keychain lives as long as the job, and codesign finds the certificate
in it. The configuration signs with the certificate and notarizes with
the profile, from that keychain in the workflow and from the login
keychain on your Mac, where `NOTARY_KEYCHAIN` is not set:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  macos: {
    signingIdentity: "Developer ID Application: Jane Doe (TEAMID)",
    notarize: { keychainProfile: "notary", keychain: process.env.NOTARY_KEYCHAIN },
  },
});
```

`mygo build` then signs the app, submits the disk image to the notary
service and waits for it, usually a few minutes, and staples the ticket.
An App Store Connect API key works instead of the Apple ID: give
`notarytool store-credentials` the key's file, ID and issuer with `--key`,
`--key-id` and `--issuer`.

## Signing Windows apps

On the Ubuntu runner, `osslsigncode` signs the Windows apps and their
installers with a `.pfx` certificate. Add it and its password to the
secrets:

```sh
base64 -i code-signing.pfx | gh secret set WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE
gh secret set WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD
```

For the Windows row, install `osslsigncode` with NSIS, write the
certificate to a file, and give its path and password to the build:

```yaml
      - name: Install NSIS and osslsigncode
        if: matrix.name == 'Windows' && runner.os == 'Linux'
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y nsis osslsigncode
      - name: Write the certificate
        if: matrix.name == 'Windows'
        env:
          WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE: ${{ secrets.WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE }}
        run: |
          echo "$WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE" | base64 --decode > "$RUNNER_TEMP/code-signing.pfx"
          echo "WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_FILE=$RUNNER_TEMP/code-signing.pfx" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Build and upload
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY }}
          MYGO_WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD }}
        run: bun run build -- -platform "${{ matrix.platform }}" -upload
```

```ts
export default defineConfig({
  windows: { certificate: process.env.WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_FILE },
});
```

The first step replaces the one that installs NSIS. Builds on your
machine, without the variable, are not signed.

### Signing on Windows

Certificates whose keys stay in a hardware token or a cloud service, such
as Azure Trusted Signing, sign with `signCommand` (see
[code signing](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/distribution.md#code-signing)), which often needs
`signtool`. Build the Windows apps on a Windows runner then, which has
`signtool`, and where `mygo build` downloads NSIS itself; the step that
installs NSIS is for Linux runners only:

```yaml
          - { name: Windows, os: windows-latest, platform: "windows/amd64,windows/arm64" }
```

Sign in to the signing service in a step for the Windows row, before
"Build and upload", as its documentation says. Steps run in PowerShell on
Windows runners unless they set `shell: bash`.

`mygo build` downloads NSIS on every run of a fresh runner. A step before
"Build and upload" keeps it in the Actions cache instead, so builds need
neither the download nor the hosts it comes from. The lockfile pins
mygo-cli, which pins NSIS:

```yaml
      - name: Cache NSIS
        if: runner.os == 'Windows'
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: ~\AppData\Local\mygo\nsis-*
          key: nsis-${{ hashFiles('bun.lock') }}
```

In a project of native UI, `go.mod` pins the CLI: key the cache on
`hashFiles('go.sum')`.

## Checking the version

A tag that does not match the configuration's version would publish the
build under another version. Keep the version in package.json, which the
configuration reads (see [computed configuration](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#computed-configuration)):

```ts
import pkg from "./package.json" with { type: "json" };

export default defineConfig({
  version: pkg.version,
});
```

and check it in the draft release job, before it creates the draft, so
that a wrong tag builds nothing:

```yaml
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Check the version
        run: test "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" = "v$(jq -r .version package.json)"
```

A project of native UI has the version in `mygo.json`: check
`jq -r .version mygo.json` instead.

## Publishing the release

Publish the draft yourself after looking at it, or let the workflow
publish it once every job uploaded:

```yaml
  publish:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: gh release edit "$GITHUB_REF_NAME" --repo "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" --draft=false
```

With a `tagPrefix` such as `desktop-v`, trigger the workflow on its tags
(`tags: ["desktop-v*"]`), check them against `desktop-v` and the version,
and create and publish the release with `--latest=false`, so the
repository's latest release stays the other releases' (see
[build and publish](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md#build-and-publish)).

Publish the tag of a prerelease, such as `v1.3.0-beta.1`, with
`--prerelease` too, so that only the apps whose users chose prereleases
update to it ([prereleases](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md#prereleases)).

## Publishing to S3

With `updates.s3`, `mygo build -upload` uploads to the bucket instead (see
[publishing to S3](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/updates.md#publishing-to-s3)). Give the jobs the
bucket's credentials in place of `GH_TOKEN`:

```yaml
        env:
          AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
          MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.MYGO_UPDATER_PRIVATE_KEY }}
```

There is no draft release: leave out the draft release job, and the
`needs` of the build job. The update of each platform is out as soon as
its job uploaded its manifest, and the workflow needs no `contents: write`
permission.

## Without a release

Without `updates`, `-upload` has nowhere to upload to. Build without it and
keep the installers as artifacts of the run, which works on every push too,
to check that the apps build:

```yaml
      - run: bun run build -- -platform "${{ matrix.platform }}"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: ${{ matrix.name }}
          path: |
            build/*/*.dmg
            build/*/*-setup-*.exe
            build/*/*.deb
            build/*/*.tar.gz
```

`build` is the `out` of new projects' configuration.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/i18n.md

# Languages

A MyGo app says its messages in the language of the people who use it.
Its messages live in catalogs, a JSON file per language, from which
`mygo dev` and `mygo build` write a Go package with a typed function per
message,
which says it in the language the app shows, with the plural forms of
that language. The whole app shows one language: its own messages,
MyGo's controls and menus, and its pages if it has any.

```json
{
  "filesSelected": "{count, plural, =0 {No files selected} one {# file selected} other {# files selected}}"
}
```

```go
ui.Text(c, locales.FilesSelected(len(app.selected))) // "3 files selected"
```

Package [`i18n`](#package-i18n) underneath formats numbers and dates
with the data of the Unicode CLDR, and an app with a frontend gets the
same messages as a TypeScript module ([In pages](#in-pages)).

## Catalogs

Turn the catalogs on in the [configuration](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#i18n), in
`mygo.json` (or `mygo.config.ts`):

```json
{
  "i18n": { "dir": "locales", "source": "en" }
}
```

`dir` (default `locales`) holds a catalog per language, named after its
[BCP 47](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/bcp47) tag: `en.json`,
`de.json`, `pt-BR.json`, `zh-Hans.json`, `zh-Hant.json`. `source`
(default `en`) is the language the app is written in: its catalog has
every message, and the others fall back to it. The languages the app
ships are the files of `dir`, which holds nothing else but Go files; an
app without catalogs ships English.

A catalog is an object of messages, in the ARB format, whose keys name
them. The source language's also describes them, under the key
with an `@`, for the translators and the generated code:

```json
{
  "@@locale": "en",
  "filesSelected": "{count, plural, =0 {No files selected} one {# file selected} other {# files selected}}",
  "@filesSelected": {
    "description": "The status bar, while files are selected.",
    "placeholders": {
      "count": { "type": "int", "example": "3" }
    }
  },
  "greeting": "Hello, {name}!"
}
```

```json
{
  "@@locale": "de",
  "filesSelected": "{count, plural, =0 {Keine Dateien ausgewählt} one {# Datei ausgewählt} other {# Dateien ausgewählt}}",
  "greeting": "Hallo, {name}!"
}
```

A key is a letter, then letters, digits and `_`; the functions of a key
are named after it. A placeholder's `type` is `String`, `int`, `double`,
`num`, `DateTime` or `Object`, which makes the type of the functions'
parameter (`string`, `int`, `float64`, `float64`, `time.Time` and `any` in
Go; `string`, `number`, `Date` and `unknown` in TypeScript). Without one,
an argument counted by `plural`, `selectordinal` or `number` is an `int`, a
`date` or `time` argument a `DateTime`, and any other a `String`. The
parameters come in the order of `placeholders`, then of the message.
`@@locale` is optional, and must name the file's language.

Keys are flat: a dot in a key is for MyGo's own strings
([`mygo.undo`](#mygos-own-strings)). Name related messages with a common
start, as `sidebarTitle`, `sidebarEmpty` and `sidebarNewNote`, which sort
together in the catalogs and in your editor's completion
(`locales.Sidebar…`).

## Messages

Messages are written in ICU MessageFormat, the format of ARB files, of
Android and of Format.JS:

| Message                                                                                              | Says                                                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Hello, {name}!`                                                                                     | the value of `name` in its place                                                                |
| `{count, plural, one {# file} other {# files}}`                                                      | the case of the plural category of `count` in the message's language; `#` is the number         |
| `{count, plural, =0 {No files} one {# file} other {# files}}`                                        | `=0` is for exactly 0, before the categories                                                    |
| `{n, plural, offset:1 =0 {Nobody} =1 {{host}} one {{host} and # other} other {{host} and # others}}` | with `offset:1`, the categories and `#` count `n - 1`                                           |
| `{place, selectordinal, one {#st} two {#nd} few {#rd} other {#th}}`                                  | the case of the ordinal category: 1st, 22nd, 103rd, 11th                                        |
| `{gender, select, female {She} male {He} other {They}} replied.`                                     | the case named after the value, else `other`                                                    |
| `{price, number}`, `{ratio, number, percent}`, `{n, number, integer}`                                | a number in the language's way (1,234.5; 1.234,5; 12,34,567)                                    |
| `{price, number, ::.00}`, `{n, number, ::group-off}`                                                 | a number with exactly two fraction digits, or without separators of thousands                   |
| `{day, date, short}`, `{day, time, short}`                                                           | a date, or a time, in a style: `short`, `medium`, `long` or `full`                              |
| `{day, date, ::yMMMd}`                                                                               | a date of the fields of a skeleton of CLDR, in the language's order (Jan 5, 2026; 5. Jan. 2026) |

Cases nest, and every `plural`, `selectordinal` and `select` has an
`other` case. A number in `{n}` is written as `{n, number}` writes it: up
to three fraction digits, grouped, in the language's digits; a number
given as a string of a decimal, `"1.50"`, keeps its fraction digits. A
plural case is the one of the number as `#` writes it, as ICU picks it:
1.0004 is written 1, whose case in English is `one`. A time in `{t}` is
written as `{t, date, short}` and `{t, time, short}` together. Numbers and
dates follow CLDR's data in Go and `Intl` in pages, which agree (see
[Formatting numbers and dates](#formatting-numbers-and-dates)). Of ICU's
number skeletons, Go and pages read `percent`, `integer`, the precision of
fraction digits (`.00`, `.0#`) and `group-off`; pages also read
`currency/EUR`, which Go writes as a plain number. The
plural categories are those of the [Unicode CLDR](https://cldr.unicode.org)
for the message's language: `one` and `other` in English, only `other`
in Chinese and Japanese, `one`, `few`, `many` and `other` in Russian, six in
Arabic. Write the ones the language has; `other` is required.

An apostrophe quotes the next brace, or `#` in a plural case: `'{'` says
`{`, `'{name}'` says `{name}`, and two apostrophes say one. Any other
apostrophe is just one, so `don't` needs no quoting.

## In Go

`mygo dev`, `mygo build` and `mygo generate` write `catalog_gen.go` into
the catalogs' directory, a Go package of its own (named after the
directory, or as its other Go files say), which embeds the catalogs:

```go
import "example.com/notes/locales"

title := locales.FilesSelected(3)                // in the language the app shows
german := locales.In("de").FilesSelected(3)      // in another
```

Each key has a function with the typed parameters of its placeholders,
which says the message in the language the app shows, and a method of
`locales.In(tag)` for another language. A message without arguments is
kept once said, so saying it again costs a map lookup and allocates
nothing: a view of native UI says its messages every frame.

The package registers its catalog with package `i18n` as it initializes,
which makes the catalogs' languages the app's: import it, with
`import _ "example.com/notes/locales"` if the Go code says no message
itself. `mygo dev` and `mygo build` warn when the app does not.

`mygo dev` writes the functions as it starts and again whenever a catalog
changes, and `mygo build` before it compiles the app; `mygo generate`
writes them alone. They are generated code: commit them with the
catalogs, so that `go build` and `go test` work without the CLI.

### When the language changes

A view of native UI is built again for every frame, so what it says
follows the language as it changes:

```go
func (app *notes) view(c *ui.Context) {
	ui.Column(c).Gap(8).Children(func() {
		ui.Text(c, locales.FilesSelected(len(app.selected)))
		if ui.Button(c, locales.NewNote()).Clicked() {
			app.add()
		}
	})
}
```

Menu items labelled by their role ("Undo", "Quit Notes") take the new
language's labels themselves. What the app set once, as a window's title
or the labels of its own menu items, it sets again when it hears the
change:

```go
win := mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{Title: locales.Title(), Content: ui.View(app.view)})
mygo.App.OnLocaleChanged(func(string) {
	win.SetTitle(locales.Title())
	mygo.App.SetMenu(app.menu()) // the menu, made again with locales' labels
})
```

## The language the app shows

The app shows one language, which `mygo.App.Locale()` returns: of the
languages it is written in, the one the user reads best, by the languages
they prefer in the order the system lists them
(`App.PreferredLanguages()`), as `zh-Hant` for a reader of `zh-TW`; else
the app's source language. An app written in English alone shows English
to a reader of Chinese, MyGo's controls and menus too, as AppKit does. The
languages the app is written in are its catalogs', which `App.SetLanguages`
replaces for an app without them.

Before 0.5, `App.Locale()` returned the user's first preferred language
whatever the app is written in. An app that translates its texts itself,
without catalogs or `App.SetLanguages`, now gets `"en"` from it: declare
its languages with `App.SetLanguages`, or read the user's from
`App.PreferredLanguages()`.

`App.SetLocale("de")` shows another language at once, and keeps it for the
next launches; `App.SetLocale("")` follows the user's languages again. A
language menu, each language named in itself ("Deutsch", "简体中文"):

```go
for _, tag := range mygo.App.Languages() {
	items = append(items, &mygo.MenuItem{Label: i18n.Autonym(tag), Type: mygo.MenuItemRadio,
		Checked: tag == mygo.App.Locale(),
		Click:   func(*mygo.MenuItem, *mygo.Window) { mygo.App.SetLocale(tag) }})
}
```

macOS keeps the language as the app's language in System Settings
(`AppleLanguages` of the app's defaults), which AppKit and WebKit say their
own texts in from the next launch; browsers keep it in `localStorage`;
Windows and Linux in the file `locale` of `App.Path(mygo.PathUserData)`.
`App.OnLocaleChanged` hears the language change, as `SetLocale` changes it
or the user's languages do (macOS, Windows and browsers report theirs;
Linux reads the environment, `LANGUAGE`, `LC_ALL`, `LC_MESSAGES` and
`LANG`, once).

When the language changes, windows of native UI draw anew, menu items
labelled by their role say the new language's labels (see
[When the language changes](#when-the-language-changes)), and pages hear
it ([In pages](#in-pages)). The app is laid out in the language's
direction, right to left in Arabic and Hebrew, unless `MYGO_DIRECTION`
(`rtl` or `ltr`) says otherwise: native UI, pages (`mygo.dir`) and, on
Linux, GTK's own widgets, as menus, agree.

### Native UI

`ui.Context.Locale()` and `ui.Context.Region()` return the app's language
and formats; a frame follows their changes. Text is drawn in the app's
language, which picks the glyphs the system's text stack draws for it, as
the Han characters Chinese and Japanese draw apart. `Element.Lang` sets the
language of an element's text and of the elements inside it, as HTML's
`lang` does, `Span.Lang` of a span of a `RichText`, `Font.Lang` of text a
`Painter` shapes:

```go
ui.Text(c, "「直」").Lang("ja") // a Japanese quote in a Chinese app
```

Han characters in a language that does not write them, as a Chinese name
in English text, keep the glyphs the system picks for the user, as
browsers do. Browsers draw the text of native UI in the page's language,
which MyGo makes the app's.

`examples/gallery` has a Languages page: a menu of languages, numbers and
dates in each, the controls in Chinese, and the pseudo locales.

### Regional formats

How dates, times and numbers are written is a setting of its own:
`App.Region()` returns the locale of the user's formats, which may be
another language's than the one the app shows, the first day of the week
and whether times have 12 or 24 hours, with the changes the user made in
the system's settings. `App.OnRegionChanged` hears them change. What the
system does not say, as a libc without the data or a browser that does
not tell, comes from CLDR's week and time data for the region
(`i18n.FirstWeekday`, `i18n.HourCycle`).

`Region.FormatLocale(language)` puts the two together as Apple's
`Locale.current` does: English read with British formats is
`en-GB-u-fw-mon-hc-h23`, with German ones `en-DE-u-fw-mon-hc-h23`; format
with it to write dates in the app's language the way the user set them:

```go
formats := mygo.App.Region().FormatLocale(mygo.App.Locale())
label := i18n.FormatDate(formats, due, i18n.DateOptions{Date: i18n.MediumStyle})
```

MyGo's date and time controls do so: the [calendar](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/calendar.md)
starts its weeks on the region's first day, the
[date input](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/date-input.md) shows the region's numeric date, the
[time input](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/time-input.md) its hour cycle, with AM and PM in the
window's language.

## Formatting numbers and dates

Package `i18n` writes numbers, dates and times as ICU and the browsers'
`Intl` write them, with the data of the Unicode CLDR for the locales of
its modern coverage (430 locales of 104 languages: `en`, `en-GB`, `de-CH`,
`pt-BR`, `zh-Hant-HK`, `ar-EG`...). A locale it has no data of formats as
the nearest it has (`zh-TW` as `zh-Hant`, `en-AU` as `en-001`), else as
English.

```go
i18n.FormatNumber("de", 1234567.891, i18n.NumberOptions{})                 // 1.234.567,891
i18n.FormatNumber("hi", 1234567, i18n.NumberOptions{})                     // 12,34,567
i18n.FormatNumber("fa", 0.25, i18n.NumberOptions{Percent: true})           // ۲۵٪
i18n.FormatNumber("en", 1.5, i18n.NumberOptions{MinFractionDigits: 2})     // 1.50
i18n.FormatDate("en", t, i18n.DateOptions{Date: i18n.FullStyle})           // Monday, January 5, 2026
i18n.FormatDate("ja", t, i18n.DateOptions{Date: i18n.LongStyle, Time: i18n.ShortStyle}) // 2026年1月5日 13:07
i18n.FormatDate("ru", t, i18n.DateOptions{Skeleton: "yMMMM"})             // январь 2026 г.
i18n.FormatDate("en", t, i18n.DateOptions{Skeleton: "jm", HourCycle: 24}) // 13:07
```

* **Numbers**: the language's separators and grouping (the Indian
  12,34,567, and none in four digits where it groups from five, as
  Spanish and Polish do), its minus and percent signs, and the digits of
  its numbering system (Arabic-Indic in Persian and Egyptian Arabic,
  Bengali in Bengali; `-u-nu-latn` asks for Latin ones). Fraction digits
  are rounded half away from zero, as `Intl` rounds them, or half to even
  (`HalfEven`). `NumberFormatter` keeps a formatter.
* **Dates and times** by style (`FullStyle` to `ShortStyle`, as
  `dateStyle` and `timeStyle`) or by **skeleton**, the fields to show in
  any order (`yMMMd`, `MMMd`, `Ed`, `jm`): the locale's pattern of CLDR
  that suits it best is found as ICU's `DateTimePatternGenerator` finds
  it, so `{year: "numeric", month: "short", day: "numeric"}` in `Intl`
  and `yMMMd` here write the same. `j` is the hour in the locale's
  cycle; `HourCycle` (or `-u-hc-h23` in the locale) makes it 12 or 24.
  Dates are in the Gregorian calendar, times in their `time.Location`.
  `DateFormatter` keeps a formatter, and `Pattern` says the pattern.
* **Names**: `Months`, `Weekdays` and `DayPeriods` in a `Width`, standing
  alone (a calendar's title, "январь") or inside a date ("января");
  `Autonym` is a language's name in itself, for a menu of languages
  ("Deutsch", "简体中文", "British English").
* **Week and clock**: `FirstWeekday` and `HourCycle` of a locale's region
  (or its language's likely one), `RegionFor` both.

Formatting allocates its result only; formatters and the locales' data
are made once and kept. The data is compressed and inflated on first use
in under a millisecond. Every app links the formatting of numbers, as
MyGo's own strings format them, with their data, about 3 KB; the
formatting of dates and their data, with the names of languages, are
linked into an app only when it formats them: with a catalog of its own
(`NewCatalog`, which `mygo generate` writes), `ParseMessage`, the
formatters or the functions that read the data. It is one package, not one per language: the
user's regional formats may be any locale's, whatever languages the app
ships.

What differs from ICU (`i18n/format_icu_test.go` lists each case the
tests skip): time zones other than UTC are written as offsets from GMT
(`GMT+8`, `GMT+05:30`) where ICU names some ("China Standard Time"); the
calendar is always the Gregorian one, where ICU's default for Thai or
Persian is another; times write spaces where CLDR has narrow no-break
ones, as V8 does; and the few locales whose data ICU 78 (CLDR 48.0) lacks
or has older (Haitian Creole, polytonic Greek) follow CLDR 48.2.

## MyGo's own strings

MyGo's controls, its code editor, diff viewer, rich text editor and
Markdown view, the terminal plugin, its document dialogs, the buttons of
pages' alert, confirm and prompt, the titles of file dialogs, and its
menus say their own words:
"Undo", "Find", "Next month", "Do you want to save the changes made to the
document “Notes”?", "Quit Notes", and the names assistive technology reads
("hours", "Saturation and brightness"). They say the language the app
shows: in native UI, the window's (`ui.Context.Locale`). An app that
ships only English shows them in English to a Chinese reader, as AppKit
does. Saying one again in the same language costs a map lookup and
allocates nothing, so controls say theirs every frame.

English is always linked. The translations to other languages, Japanese (`ja`),
Simplified Chinese (`zh-Hans`) and Traditional Chinese (`zh-Hant`) so far, are
packages of their own, so that an app carries only those of the languages
it ships. The code `mygo generate` writes for an app's catalogs imports
them for the app's languages: an app with a `zh-TW.json` gets MyGo's
`zh-Hant`. An app without catalogs, which sets its languages with
`App.SetLanguages`, imports them itself:

```go
import _ "github.com/egoist/mygo/locales/zh-Hans"
```

An app that ships a language MyGo is translated to without importing the
translation is told so as it starts, and shows MyGo's strings in English
there. An app changes MyGo's strings, or gives them its other languages,
with keys `mygo.<key>` in its catalogs:

```json
{
  "mygo.undo": "Rückgängig",
  "mygo.menuQuitApp": "{app} beenden"
}
```

The keys, their messages and their arguments are MyGo's catalog,
[internal/l10n/en.json](https://github.com/egoist/mygo/blob/main/internal/l10n/en.json).
A string resolves as the app's own do: in the app's language, then the
languages it falls back to, then the app's source language, then English.
The inspector of native UI, a tool of developers, stays in English.

### Adding a language to MyGo

MyGo's own strings are `internal/l10n/en.json`, and each translation is
`locales/<tag>/<tag>.json`. To translate MyGo to a language, add
`locales/<tag>/<tag>.json` with every key of `en.json` (the descriptions
say where each shows), run `go generate ./internal/l10n`, which writes the
translation's package and adds it to the languages `mygo generate` links
for apps, and `go test ./internal/l10n`, which checks it as `mygo generate`
checks an app's catalogs: every message in every language, with the
source's placeholders and the language's plural cases.
`mygo.appName` and `mygo.appDescription` are the app's name and
description in a language, which packaging writes where systems list the
app (see [building and distributing](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/distribution.md#languages)).

## Which message

A message is the one of the catalog's language that suits the language
asked for best: `zh-Hant` for `zh-TW`, `pt-PT` for `pt-AO`, `en-GB` for
`en-AU`. When that language lacks it, it falls back along CLDR's parent
locales (`en-AU`, `en-001`, `en`; `zh-Hant-HK`, `zh-Hant`), then to the
source language: a missing translation says the source's message rather
than nothing. Its plural cases follow the rules of the language the
message is written in; numbers and dates, the conventions of the language
asked for.

## Checking the catalogs

`mygo generate` and `mygo build` check the catalogs, and so does
`mygo i18n check`. Errors stop them:

* a file not named after a canonical tag, or whose `@@locale` differs;
* a message that does not parse;
* a key a translation has and the source does not, or a key `mygo.<key>`
  MyGo has no message for;
* an argument a translation has and the source's message does not, or used
  in a way its type cannot be (a `String` counted by `plural`);
* two keys whose functions would have the same name.

Warnings do not: messages a translation lacks, which say the source
language's; arguments it leaves out; plural cases its language does not
have (`few` in English) or lacks (`few` in Russian, which says `other` in
its place); placeholders a message does not use.

## Trying a language

`mygo dev -lang de` runs the app in German without changing the language
it keeps. Two pseudo locales test layouts before any translation exists,
as Android's do:

* `en-XA` accents the letters of the source language's messages, makes them
  a third longer and brackets them, `[Šéļéçţ ƒîļéš one two]`: text that
  stays plain is not in a catalog, cut text is too short a space, and a
  sentence of several brackets is made of pieces a translation cannot
  reorder.
* `ar-XB` shows each word right to left, and lays the app out right to
  left: what does not mirror shows.

## In pages

An app with a frontend says the same messages in its pages. Next to the
[TypeScript client](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/bindings.md#the-generated-client), the CLI writes a
module named after the catalogs' directory, such as
`src/locales.ts`, with a typed function per key; an app without a
frontend gets none.

```ts
import { languages, messages, messagesIn } from "./locales";

heading.textContent = messages.filesSelected(3); // in the language the page shows
messagesIn("de").greeting("Ada");                 // "Hallo, Ada!"
```

The module holds the messages of every language, and `mygo-runtime/i18n`
formats them with the browser's `Intl`, so the pages and Go say the same
words in the same plural forms. The messages are bundled with the
frontend rather than fetched: the first paint is in the right language,
without waiting for a request, also in a page of the dev server opened in
a browser. `messages` says each message in the language of the moment:
the app's, which MyGo gives the page before its scripts run, else the
browser's.

`mygo.locale` and `mygo.dir` are there before the page's scripts run.
When the language changes, pages hear the `mygo:locale` event
(`onLocaleChange` of `mygo-runtime`): draw the page again. Pages loaded
later start in the new language. Web views take the language too, for
their own texts: WebView2 as its environment is made, which keeps it (a
change shows from the next launch), WebKitGTK at once, WKWebView from the
next launch.

`formatMessage(locale, message, args)` from `mygo-runtime/i18n` formats a
message of your own.

## Package i18n

The generated code is built on package
[`i18n`](https://pkg.go.dev/github.com/egoist/mygo/i18n), which apps can
use directly: `NewCatalog` reads catalogs from any `fs.FS`, `ParseMessage`
and `Message.Format` format a message, `PluralCategory` and
`OrdinalCategory` give the CLDR plural category of a number, written as an
integer, a float or a decimal string whose fraction digits count (`"1.50"`
has two), `Parent` the locale a locale falls back to, and the formatting
of [numbers and dates](#formatting-numbers-and-dates). Its data comes from
CLDR `i18n.CLDRVersion`.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/launchers.md

# Launchers

A launcher, as Spotlight, Raycast, Alfred, PowerToys Run or Ulauncher, is
summoned from anywhere with a keyboard shortcut, takes what the user types
over the app they are in, and goes away as fast as it came. MyGo has the
parts: a [panel](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#panels) to show it in, a
[global shortcut](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md#global-shortcuts) to summon it, the
[installed apps](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md#the-shell) and their icons to search, and an app
without a Dock icon that lives in the [tray](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/menus.md#tray-icons).
[`examples/launcher`](https://github.com/egoist/mygo/tree/main/examples/launcher)
puts them together in native UI:

```sh
go run ./examples/launcher
```

## An app in the background

A launcher has no Dock icon and no entry in the app switcher, runs with
no window showing, and runs once:

```go
func main() {
	if !mygo.App.RequestSingleInstanceLock() {
		return // the launcher that runs shows itself
	}
	mygo.App.SetActivationPolicy(mygo.ActivationPolicyAccessory)
	mygo.App.OnWindowAllClosed(func() {})
	mygo.App.OnSecondInstance(func([]string, string) { show() })
	mygo.App.WhenReady(ready)
	if err := mygo.App.Run(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

A packaged app says it from the start, so that macOS never shows it in the
Dock, with `LSUIElement` in [`mygo.json`](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/configuration.md#mygojson):

```json
{
  "macos": { "infoPlist": { "LSUIElement": true } }
}
```

A tray icon gives the user a way in other than the shortcut, and to quit;
[`App.SetOpenAtLogin`](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/app.md#start-at-login) starts the launcher with the
session, and `App.WasOpenedAtLogin` tells it to stay hidden then.

## The panel

A panel floats above every app, full-screen ones too, on whichever Space
or virtual desktop the user is on, and on macOS takes the keyboard without
activating the launcher: the app the user was in keeps its menu bar, and
has the keyboard back once the panel hides. Create it hidden, once, and
hide it rather than close it, so that it shows again at once, as it was:

```go
panel := mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{
	Panel:         true,
	Hidden:        true,
	Frameless:     true,
	Transparent:   true,
	Vibrancy:      mygo.VibrancyGlass, // Liquid Glass on macOS 26, Acrylic on Windows 11
	CornerRadius:  16,
	Width:         680,
	Height:        420,
	DisableResize: true,
	Content:       ui.View(app.view), // or URL: "/launcher"
})
panel.OnClose(func(e *mygo.CloseEvent) { // Escape, Cmd-W, Alt-F4
	e.PreventDefault()
	panel.Hide()
})
panel.OnBlur(panel.Hide) // the user went elsewhere
```

An Escape that the page or native UI leaves closes a panel, which the
`OnClose` listener turns into hiding it. Handle Escape yourself where it
does something first, as clearing the query does in the example.

Show it on the display the user is looking at, which the pointer tells,
a third of the way down as Spotlight does, and give its search field the
keyboard:

```go
func show() {
	d := mygo.Screen.DisplayNearestPoint(mygo.Screen.CursorScreenPoint())
	w, h := panel.Size()
	panel.SetPosition(d.WorkArea.X+(d.WorkArea.Width-w)/2, d.WorkArea.Y+(d.WorkArea.Height-h)/3)
	app.query = ""
	app.input.Focus()
	panel.Show()
}
```

## The shortcut

```go
err := mygo.GlobalShortcut.Register("Alt+Shift+Space", func() {
	if panel.IsVisible() {
		panel.Hide()
	} else {
		show()
	}
})
```

Pick one other launchers leave free: Raycast and PowerToys Run take
Alt+Space, Spotlight Cmd+Space, and macOS gives a shortcut to every app
that registers it, so both would open. Let the user choose another in the
launcher's settings: `Unregister` the old one and `Register` the new one,
and tell them when `Register` fails because it is taken. On Windows the
key press lets the panel take the foreground; on Wayland the desktop binds
the shortcut, see [global shortcuts](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md#global-shortcuts).

## Finding apps

`Shell.InstalledApps` lists the applications installed on the computer,
sorted by name, with the names the system shows in the user's language.
It reads the disk, in tens of milliseconds: list them on a goroutine as
the panel shows, and hand them to the view with `Window.Update` (or to the
page through a bound service):

```go
go func() {
	apps, err := mygo.Shell.InstalledApps()
	if err != nil {
		log.Print(err)
	}
	panel.Update(func() {
		app.apps = apps
		app.filter()
	})
}()
```

`Shell.FileIcon(app.Path, size)` draws an app's icon as a PNG, in pixels:
the size in DIPs times the scale factor of the display. It takes a few
milliseconds: draw the icons of the rows that show, and keep them by path.
`Shell.LaunchApp(app)` starts the chosen app, or brings it to the front;
hide the panel first, so that the app the user was in has the keyboard
until the launched one takes it.

## Platforms

|                                 | macOS                                                                                | Windows                   | Linux                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| no Dock icon, no taskbar button | `LSUIElement`, `ActivationPolicyAccessory`                                           | a panel has none          | a panel has none                                                                                                        |
| the panel                       | a nonactivating `NSPanel`, over full-screen apps of regular and accessory apps alike | a topmost tool window     | a utility window kept above on X11; a layer surface where Wayland compositors have one (with `libgtk-layer-shell.so.0`) |
| the shortcut                    | Carbon hot keys                                                                      | `RegisterHotKey`          | X11 grabs, the XDG desktop portal under Wayland                                                                         |
| the apps                        | the Applications folders                                                             | the Start menu's All apps | desktop entries                                                                                                         |

On Wayland, a panel that is a layer surface keeps the keyboard while it
shows, as launchers there do, so it is blurred only as it hides: close it
on Escape.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/menus.md

# Menus and the tray

Menus are built from templates of `*mygo.MenuItem` and used as the menu
bar, context menus, the Dock menu and the menus of tray icons.

## Templates

```go
menu := mygo.NewMenu([]*mygo.MenuItem{
	{Role: mygo.RoleAppMenu},
	{Label: "File", Submenu: []*mygo.MenuItem{
		{Label: "New Note", Accelerator: "CmdOrCtrl+N", Click: func(item *mygo.MenuItem, win *mygo.Window) {
			newNote()
		}},
		{Label: "Export…", Accelerator: "CmdOrCtrl+E", Click: exportNotes},
		mygo.Separator(),
		{Role: mygo.RoleClose},
	}},
	{Role: mygo.RoleEditMenu},
	{Label: "View", Submenu: []*mygo.MenuItem{
		{ID: "sidebar", Label: "Show Sidebar", Type: mygo.MenuItemCheckbox, Checked: true, Click: toggleSidebar},
		mygo.Separator(),
		{Label: "List", Type: mygo.MenuItemRadio, Checked: true},
		{Label: "Grid", Type: mygo.MenuItemRadio},
		mygo.Separator(),
		{Role: mygo.RoleToggleDevTools},
		{Role: mygo.RoleToggleFullScreen},
	}},
	{Role: mygo.RoleWindowMenu},
})
```

A `MenuItem` has:

* `Label`, and an `Accelerator`, its keyboard shortcut (see
  [accelerators](#accelerators));
* `Click`, called on the main thread when the item is chosen, with the item
  and, on Linux and Windows, the window whose menu bar or context menu was
  chosen. Other menus use the focused window, or nil;
* `Type`: `MenuItemNormal`, `MenuItemCheckbox`, `MenuItemRadio`,
  `MenuItemSeparator` or `MenuItemSubmenu`; items with a `Submenu` are
  submenus, others normal items unless set. Adjacent radio items form a
  group, in which checking one unchecks the others. Checkbox and radio
  items toggle `Checked` before `Click` runs;
* `Disabled`, `Hidden` and `ToolTip`;
* `Icon`, an image shown beside the label (see [icons](#icons));
* `ID`, to find the item with `Menu.ItemByID`;
* `Role`, a built-in behavior with its label and accelerator.

### Roles

Roles do what users expect of standard items, with their usual label and
shortcut, which `Label` and `Accelerator` override:

* editing: `RoleUndo`, `RoleRedo`, `RoleCut`, `RoleCopy`, `RolePaste`,
  `RoleDelete`, `RoleSelectAll`, and on macOS `RolePasteAndMatchStyle`.
  Their keys go to the content first, as in a browser: in a page on
  Windows, WebView2 cuts, copies and pastes with the page's own events and
  every format of the clipboard, while choosing Paste from the menu types
  the clipboard's text, as pages may not read the clipboard (as does an
  edit role given a key the page has no use for, as Copy on Ctrl+Shift+C);
* formatting: `RoleBold`, `RoleItalic`, `RoleUnderline`,
  `RoleStrikethrough`, `RoleAlignLeft`, `RoleAlignCenter` and
  `RoleAlignRight`, which format the selection of a [rich text
  editor](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/rich-text-editor.md) of native UI, or of an editable page
  (`document.execCommand`); Paste and Match Style pastes plain text into a
  rich text editor;
* the page: `RoleReload`, `RoleForceReload`, `RoleToggleDevTools` (in a
  window of native UI, its [inspector](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/inspector.md)),
  `RoleResetZoom`, `RoleZoomIn`, `RoleZoomOut`;
* the window: `RoleToggleFullScreen`, `RoleMinimize`, `RoleZoom`,
  `RoleClose`;
* [documents](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/documents.md#the-file-menu): `RoleNew`, `RoleOpen`,
  `RoleOpenRecent`, `RoleSave`, `RoleSaveAs`, `RoleDuplicate`,
  `RoleRename`, `RoleMoveTo`, `RoleRevert`;
* the app: `RoleQuit`, and on macOS `RoleAbout`, `RoleHide`,
  `RoleHideOthers`, `RoleUnhide`, `RoleFront`, `RoleServices`,
  `RoleStartSpeaking`, `RoleStopSpeaking`;
* whole menus: `RoleFileMenu`, `RoleEditMenu`, `RoleFormatMenu` (Bold,
  Italic, Underline, Strikethrough and the alignments), `RoleViewMenu` and
  `RoleWindowMenu`, and on macOS `RoleAppMenu` (the menu named after the
  app), `RoleWindow` (the menu listing the windows) and `RoleHelp` (the
  menu with the search field).

Items with the roles of macOS are left out on other platforms, so one
template serves every platform.

### Changing items

Change items of a menu in use with their methods, so that the native menu
follows: `SetLabel`, `SetEnabled`, `SetVisible`, `SetChecked`,
`SetAccelerator` and `SetIcon`:

```go
item := menu.ItemByID("sidebar")
item.SetChecked(false)
```

`Menu.Append` and `Menu.Insert` add items.

### Icons

An item's `Icon` is an image shown beside its label, as the flag of each
server of a VPN's tray menu. `NewMenuIcon` makes one of a PNG image, in
its own colors, and returns an error for data that is not a PNG image;
make each once and give it to as many items as show it:

```go
//go:embed flags/jp.png
var japanPNG []byte

japan, err := mygo.NewMenuIcon(japanPNG, false)
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
servers := mygo.NewMenu([]*mygo.MenuItem{
	{ID: "tokyo", Label: "Tokyo", Type: mygo.MenuItemRadio, Checked: true, Icon: japan},
	{ID: "osaka", Label: "Osaka", Type: mygo.MenuItemRadio, Icon: japan},
	{ID: "direct", Label: "Direct", Type: mygo.MenuItemRadio},
})
```

The image fits a box of 16 by 16 points, keeping its aspect: give it at
least 32 by 32 pixels, or 48 by 48, so that it stays sharp on
high-resolution displays and at 150% and 200% scaling. A checkbox or radio
item shows its check as well. `SetIcon`
replaces an item's icon in menus in use, and nil removes it:

```go
servers.ItemByID("tokyo").SetIcon(warning)
servers.ItemByID("osaka").SetIcon(nil)
```

`NewMenuIcon`'s second argument, template, makes a black and transparent
image take the color of the menu's text, as macOS tints its template
images: white in a dark menu and on the highlight. Linux shows template
icons as they are.

MyGo decodes and scales each image once, however many items show it and
however often their menus open or are made again, the icons of the same
image included, and frees what it made of it once neither the app nor a
menu holds the icon; the bitmaps of Windows 10's menus go with their
menus. Apps that make no icon don't link the code that draws them.

* **macOS** shows the icon (an `NSImage`) after the column of checks, on
  every menu, the menu bar's own items included, which show it in the
  menu bar.
* **Windows 11** menus, which MyGo draws, give icons a column of their
  own between the checks and the labels, as the system's menus do, at the
  menu's display scaling. **Windows 10** draws them as the items'
  bitmaps (32-bit, with alpha), in the column of its checks: a checked
  item shows its icon framed as checked in place of a check mark. The
  items of the menu bar itself show no icon.
* **Linux** shows icons in the items of menu bars' menus and context
  menus (GTK); the items of the menu bar itself show none. A tray icon's
  menu is drawn by the panel, which gets the icons over DBusMenu
  (`icon-data`): GNOME Shell's AppIndicator extension and KDE Plasma
  show them, other panels may not.

## The menu bar

```go
mygo.App.SetMenu(menu)
```

On macOS the menu bar belongs to the app. Apps get a default one, with the
app, File, Edit, View and Window menus, until they set their own: keep
`RoleAppMenu` and `RoleEditMenu` in yours, which make Cmd+Q and copy and
paste work.

On Linux and Windows menu bars belong to windows. `App.SetMenu` gives its
menu to every window without one of its own, `Window.SetMenu` gives a
window its own, and windows have none by default, except in apps with
[documents](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/documents.md), which get File and Edit menus. `App.SetMenu(nil)`
removes the menu.

On Windows, menu bars and menus follow the appearance, light or dark, as
the title bar does (see [dark mode](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/frontend.md#dark-mode)). On Windows 11
they look like the system's own menus, as File Explorer's: roomier items,
highlights with rounded corners, and shortcuts in a fainter color.

A window with `AutoHideMenuBar` keeps its menu bar out of sight, and the
room for the page. Alt pressed alone, or F10, shows the bar with the
keyboard in it (Windows) or its first menu open (Linux), and the bar hides
again once the user picks an item or leaves it. Its shortcuts work all
along:

```go
mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{URL: "/", AutoHideMenuBar: true})
```

A Windows window without a title bar, frameless or with a hidden title
bar, has no room for a menu bar either: Alt and F10 open its menus in a
popup from the top-left corner, below the title bar the page draws. On
Linux a window with a hidden title bar hides its menu bar as
`AutoHideMenuBar` does, so that the window buttons stay at the top of the
window, in the page's title bar; a frameless window shows the bar above
the page.

A window in full screen leaves the whole screen to the page: its menu bar
hides until it leaves full screen. Alt and F10 still open its menus, in a
popup from the top-left corner on Windows, and in the bar, which shows
while they are open, on Linux.

## Context menus

`Menu.Popup` shows a menu at the mouse over a window and returns once it
closes; `PopupAt` shows it at a position in the page. Show one from a bound
method, which the page calls on right-click:

```go
// ShowNoteMenu shows the context menu of a note.
func (n *Notes) ShowNoteMenu(ctx context.Context, id int64) {
	menu := mygo.NewMenu([]*mygo.MenuItem{
		{Label: "Rename", Click: func(*mygo.MenuItem, *mygo.Window) { n.startRename(id) }},
		{Label: "Delete", Click: func(*mygo.MenuItem, *mygo.Window) { n.Delete(id) }},
	})
	menu.Popup(mygo.CallerWindow(ctx))
}
```

```ts
note.addEventListener("contextmenu", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  Notes.showNoteMenu(id);
});
```

Without a handler of their own, pages show the webview's standard context
menu, with Copy and Paste on text and Inspect Element in development
builds. Windows showing [native UI](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/context-menu.md) give elements context
menus with `ContextMenu`, built like the rest of their interface.

## The Dock menu

On macOS `App.Dock.SetMenu` adds items above the standard ones of the menu
that right-clicking the Dock icon opens. Like `App.SetMenu`, it may be
called in `main` before `App.Run`:

```go
mygo.App.Dock.SetMenu(mygo.NewMenu([]*mygo.MenuItem{
	{Label: "New Window", Click: func(*mygo.MenuItem, *mygo.Window) { openMainWindow() }},
}))
```

## Tray icons

A tray icon sits in the menu bar on macOS and in the notification area on
Windows and Linux. Create one once the app is ready:

```go
//go:embed resources/tray.png
var trayIcon []byte

mygo.App.WhenReady(func() {
	tray, err := mygo.NewTray(mygo.TrayOptions{
		Icon:           trayIcon,
		IconIsTemplate: true, // macOS tints it to match the menu bar
		ToolTip:        "Notes",
		Menu: mygo.NewMenu([]*mygo.MenuItem{
			{Label: "Open Notes", Click: func(*mygo.MenuItem, *mygo.Window) { openMainWindow() }},
			mygo.Separator(),
			{Role: mygo.RoleQuit},
		}),
	})
	if err != nil {
		log.Println("tray:", err)
	}
	_ = tray
})
```

The icon is a PNG, ideally 16×16 points (a 32×32 image for high-resolution
displays); a template icon, black on transparent, lets macOS tint it for
light and dark menu bars. A tray with a menu shows it on click. Without a
menu, clicks reach `OnClick`, and `OnRightClick` gets right-clicks. Change
the tray with `SetIcon`, `SetMenu`, `SetToolTip` and, on macOS,
`SetTitle`, the text next to the icon; `Destroy` removes it.

The items of a tray's menu can show [icons](#icons), as a country's flag
beside each server, and change as the items of any menu do: the menu
shows their state the next time it opens.

A title that shows a changing number, such as a network speed, should
keep its width, or the item grows and shrinks and the icon and the items
beside it move. On macOS the title's digits all have the same width, so a
value padded to a fixed number of characters keeps it: pad with figure
spaces (U+2007), which are as wide as a digit, since an ordinary space is
narrower.

```go
// "  9.0 MB/s", " 12.5 MB/s", "128.0 MB/s": all as wide.
func speed(mbps float64) string {
	return strings.ReplaceAll(fmt.Sprintf("%5.1f", mbps), " ", "\u2007") + " MB/s"
}

tray.SetTitle(speed(rate))
```

Only digits are tabular: letters keep their own widths, so a title that
switches units (`9 KB/s`, then `1.2 MB/s`) changes width with the unit.
Keeping that steady is the app's choice, by showing the value in one unit
as above, for one.

An app may show several icons, as a menu bar app showing its measures each
in an item of its own. On macOS a new icon goes left of those already
there, and the user moves icons by dragging them with ⌘ held: give each an
`ID`, unique among the app's icons, and it goes back where the user put it
whenever it is made again, at the next launch or after `Destroy`. On
Windows, where the user chooses which icons show on the taskbar rather
than in its overflow, an icon with an `ID` keeps that choice, whatever
order the app makes its icons in.

A template icon follows the menu bar by itself. An icon in color, as one
drawing each of its measures in its own color, draws its ink for the bar
it shows on: `Tray.Dark` reports whether that bar is dark (the macOS menu
bar, as the system's appearance or the wallpaper under it tints it, or the
Windows taskbar), and `OnAppearanceChange` tells when it turns, to set the
icon again:

```go
draw := func() { tray.SetIcon(meterIcon(tray.Dark()), false) }
tray.OnAppearanceChange(draw)
draw()
```

`Tray.PopUpMenu` opens the menu set with `SetMenu` programmatically. On
macOS, AppKit places it below the status item and highlights its button
while the menu is open. To show a menu only on right-click while keeping
primary clicks available, set the menu in `OnRightClick`, call
`PopUpMenu`, then clear it with `SetMenu(nil)` when the call returns.

A tray icon does not keep the app running: the app quits when its last
window closes ([Quitting](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/app.md#quitting)). To close a window to the
tray, hide it instead, which keeps the window and the app. A quit, as the
tray menu's `RoleQuit`, starts before the windows close, so `OnClose` can
tell the closes it makes from the user's:

```go
var quitting bool // OnBeforeQuit and OnClose run on the main thread
mygo.App.OnBeforeQuit(func(*mygo.QuitEvent) { quitting = true })

win.OnClose(func(e *mygo.CloseEvent) {
	if !quitting {
		e.PreventDefault()
		win.Hide()
	}
})
// The icon's click, without a menu, or an item of its menu, brings it back.
tray.OnClick(win.Show)
```

On Linux tray icons use AppIndicator, which needs
`libayatana-appindicator3`: they show a menu, and an icon with an `OnClick`
listener answers activation (with a release of the library that has the
`activate` signal; older ones report no clicks), which GNOME's AppIndicator extension sends on
a double click and which opens the menu on a single one after the double
click time. `NewTray` returns an error without the library.

Apps that live in the menu bar usually drop their Dock icon on macOS:

```go
mygo.App.SetActivationPolicy(mygo.ActivationPolicyAccessory)
```

For an icon that opens a window of native UI, see
[the menu bar example](https://github.com/egoist/mygo/tree/main/examples/menubar-native).
It leaves the tray menu unset on macOS and Windows, uses `OnClick` to
toggle a frameless window positioned with `Tray.Bounds`, and hides it on
`OnBlur` or Escape. On Linux, an AppIndicator menu item opens the same
window.

## Accelerators

Accelerators are keys with modifiers joined by `+`, such as `CmdOrCtrl+N`
or `Alt+Shift+F4`, in any case.

Modifiers:

| Modifier                                  | Key                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| `CmdOrCtrl` (`CommandOrControl`)          | Command on macOS, Control elsewhere                  |
| `Cmd` (`Command`), `Super`, `Meta`, `Win` | Command on macOS, the Windows or Super key elsewhere |
| `Ctrl` (`Control`)                        | Control                                              |
| `Alt` (`Option`, `AltGr`)                 | Alt, or Option on macOS                              |
| `Shift`                                   | Shift                                                |

Keys:

* a character: a letter, a digit or a sign such as `,` or `/` (`Plus` for
  `+`);
* `F1` to `F24`;
* `Enter` (`Return`), `Tab`, `Space`, `Backspace`, `Delete` (`Del`),
  `Insert` (`Ins`), `Escape` (`Esc`);
* `Up`, `Down`, `Left`, `Right`, `Home`, `End`, `PageUp`, `PageDown`;
* `Num0` to `Num9`, `NumDec`, `NumAdd`, `NumSub`, `NumMult`, `NumDiv` (the
  numeric keypad);
* `VolumeUp`, `VolumeDown`, `VolumeMute`, `MediaPlayPause`,
  `MediaNextTrack`, `MediaPreviousTrack`, `MediaStop`, `PrintScreen`,
  `CapsLock`, `NumLock`, `ScrollLock`.

The same syntax registers [global shortcuts](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md#global-shortcuts).

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md

# Desktop APIs

MyGo wraps the parts of the operating system desktop apps use most, for
apps whose windows show web pages, native UI or both. Like the rest of
MyGo, each can be called from any goroutine.

## Dialogs

`mygo.Dialog` shows the system's file and message dialogs. Its methods
block until the user answers: call them from bound methods, which run on
goroutines of their own, or start a goroutine for them in event listeners
and menu items, which should return quickly. `Parent` attaches a dialog to a
window, as a sheet on macOS.

```go
// Pick files.
paths, err := mygo.Dialog.Open(mygo.OpenDialogOptions{
	Parent:   win,
	Title:    "Import",
	Filters:  []mygo.FileFilter{{Name: "Images", Extensions: []string{"png", "jpg"}}},
	Multiple: true,
}) // nil when canceled

// Choose where to save.
path, err := mygo.Dialog.Save(mygo.SaveDialogOptions{
	Parent:      win,
	DefaultPath: "notes.json",
}) // "" when canceled

// Ask a question.
res, err := mygo.Dialog.Message(mygo.MessageOptions{
	Parent:        win,
	Type:          mygo.MessageWarning,
	Message:       "Delete 3 notes?",
	Detail:        "You cannot undo this.",
	Buttons:       []string{"Delete", "Cancel"},
	CheckboxLabel: "Don't ask again",
})
if res.Button == 0 { /* Delete */ }

// Report an error.
mygo.Dialog.Error("Import failed", err.Error())
```

`OpenDialogOptions` also pick directories (`Directory`), show hidden files
and, on macOS, a message and a New Folder button. In message dialogs Enter
activates `DefaultButton` and Escape `CancelButton`, by default the first
button labeled Cancel or No.

## Notifications

```go
n := mygo.NewNotification(mygo.NotificationOptions{
	Title: "Export finished",
	Body:  "notes.json was saved to Documents.",
})
n.OnClick(func() { mainWindow().Focus() })
if err := n.Show(); err != nil {
	log.Println(err)
}
```

`Close` removes a notification. macOS shows notifications of packaged apps
only, which `mygo dev` and `mygo build` make; `mygo.NotificationsSupported()`
reports whether the app can show them. Linux shows them through the
desktop's notification service, Windows as notification-area balloons.
`Show` returns once the system has the notification. On macOS the first
one asks the user whether to allow notifications, and `Show` waits for the
answer; it returns `mygo.ErrNotificationsDenied` when they are not allowed,
by that answer or later in System Settings.

macOS keeps a notification in Notification Center after it is clicked,
until the app removes it: `Close` it in `OnClick` to take it away, or call
`mygo.ClearNotifications()`, which removes all of the app's notifications,
those of earlier runs too, as the app comes to the front:

```go
n.OnClick(func() {
	mainWindow().Focus()
	n.Close()
})

// What the user has seen in the app does not wait in Notification Center.
mygo.App.OnDidBecomeActive(func() { mygo.ClearNotifications() })
```

Linux asks the desktop's notification service to close them, which may
have closed them already, and Windows hides its balloon.

A notification can outlive the run that showed it, in Notification Center
on macOS, where a click launches the app again. Give it an `ID` of the
app's own, which `App.OnNotificationClick` receives for every click, that
one included when it is registered before `Run`; showing a notification
with the `ID` of one still shown replaces it. `Group` gathers notifications
in one stack of Notification Center, such as the messages of a
conversation (macOS):

```go
// IDs are "<conversation>/<message>".
mygo.App.OnNotificationClick(func(id string) {
	conversation, _, _ := strings.Cut(id, "/")
	openConversation(conversation)
})

mygo.NewNotification(mygo.NotificationOptions{
	ID:    "ada/" + msg.ID,
	Group: "ada",
	Title: "Ada",
	Body:  msg.Text,
}).Show()
```

### Sender avatars on macOS

An incoming direct message can supply a sender to display a prominent
avatar with the app's small icon on macOS 12 and later:

```go
mygo.NewNotification(mygo.NotificationOptions{
	ID: "message:7", Group: "conversation:3",
	Title: "Ada", Subtitle: "Lunch", Body: "See you at noon",
	Sender: &mygo.NotificationSender{
		ID: "user:ada", Name: "Ada", Avatar: avatarPNG,
	},
}).Show()
```

`Sender.ID` identifies the person in the app; it is not inferred to be an
email address or phone number. `Name` defaults to `Title`. `Avatar` holds
encoded image bytes, such as PNG, JPEG or SVG; macOS rasterizes them as PNG
before donation. The app fetches them and decides
whether the message's sender and content may be shared with the system.
`NewNotification` copies the sender and image, so the app can reuse its
buffers. `Group` is the conversation identifier; without one, it uses the
notification's ID. This API represents a direct incoming message, not a
group chat or outgoing message. macOS controls the communication layout;
the subtitle is included above the message in the body.

Enable **Communication Notifications** for the app's Apple App ID and add
`INSendMessageIntent` to `macos.infoPlist.NSUserActivityTypes`. Sign with
`com.apple.developer.usernotifications.communication` and embed a matching
provisioning profile, including for Developer ID distribution: set
`macos.provisioningProfile`, which `mygo build` copies to
`Contents/embedded.provisionprofile` before signing (see
[Provisioning profiles](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/distribution.md#provisioning-profiles)). The
profile must authorize the app's identifier, certificate and entitlements.
Do not add the restricted entitlement to an ad-hoc build: macOS can refuse
to launch it.

MyGo checks the signed entitlement before donating the incoming message to
SiriKit and updating its notification content. Without the capability, with
an incomplete sender or invalid avatar, or when donation/content conversion
fails, it sends the ordinary notification. Windows, Linux and unsupported
platforms retain their existing behavior. IDs, sound, grouping, click
handlers, `Close` and `ClearNotifications` use the same notification lifecycle.

## Clipboard

```go
mygo.Clipboard.WriteText("hello")
text := mygo.Clipboard.ReadText()

mygo.Clipboard.WriteHTML("<b>hello</b>")
mygo.Clipboard.WriteImage(png) // a PNG
img := mygo.Clipboard.ReadImage()

formats := mygo.Clipboard.AvailableFormats()
mygo.Clipboard.Clear()
```

Pages can use the web's `navigator.clipboard` too.

`Clipboard.Write(transfer.Data)` and `Clipboard.Read(formats...)` share the
native drag/drop model: ordered items, alternative representations, file
lists, custom MIME formats, and lazy providers. `Formats` discovers portable
names without requesting bytes; `ReadFormat`, `ReadFiles`, `WriteFiles`, and
`Flush` provide explicit negotiation, file transfer, and persistence. See
[Clipboard and drag data](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/data-transfer.md) for provider lifetimes and native
format mappings. The [clipboard example](https://github.com/egoist/mygo/tree/main/examples/clipboard) demonstrates
these operations.

## The shell

```go
mygo.Shell.OpenExternal("https://example.com") // the default browser
mygo.Shell.OpenPath("/Users/ada/report.pdf")   // the default app for the file
mygo.Shell.ShowItemInFolder(path)              // Finder, Explorer, the file manager
mygo.Shell.TrashItem(path)                     // to the trash
mygo.Shell.Beep()
```

`TrashItem` never deletes for good: when the item cannot go to the trash
it fails and leaves the item where it is. On Windows that is an item too
big for the recycle bin, or on a drive without one, as network shares and
many removable drives are, which Windows would otherwise delete without
asking.

`FileIcon` returns the icon the file manager shows for a file, a folder
or an application, as a PNG of the size asked for in pixels: pass the size
in DIPs times the display's scale factor.

```go
png, err := mygo.Shell.FileIcon("/Applications/Safari.app", 64)
```

On macOS it is Finder's icon (`NSWorkspace`), drawn from the
representation that fits the size best; a symbolic link has the icon of
what it points to, without Finder's arrow. On Windows it is Explorer's
(`IShellItemImageFactory`, icons only, no thumbnails), and the path may
also name a shell item, such as an app of the Start menu by
`shell:AppsFolder\<AppUserModelID>`. On Linux it is the icon of the file's
content type from the icon theme, and for a desktop entry (`.desktop`), the
icon of its application, or where the theme has none, that of desktop
entries.

`InstalledApps` lists the applications installed on the computer, sorted
by name, as a launcher shows them, and `LaunchApp` starts one, or brings
it to the front:

```go
go func() {
	apps, err := mygo.Shell.InstalledApps() // reads the disk: off the main thread
	if err != nil {
		return
	}
```
