# Migrating to checked elements

Native UI views receive `*ui.Context`, child builders use `func()` callbacks,
and widget constructors return `ui.Element` values. This guide covers source
migration, build lifetimes, persistent control identity and focus bindings.

## Apply the source migration

Run the migration from your app directory:

```sh
go tool mygo migrate-ui .          # preview affected files
go tool mygo migrate-ui -write .   # write the source migration
go tool mygo vet .
go test ./...
```

Review the diff before committing it. The codemod uses Go syntax and the
actual UI import alias, sharing field and helper-return declarations across
files in the same package. It converts element and custom-parts pointer types,
element nil checks and zero assignments, moves fluent constructor keys into
`Context.Key`, and renames grid `Rows(n)` to `GridRows(n)`. Context pointers,
child callback signatures, ordinary model pointers and unrelated nil checks
are preserved. Dot imports and keys on separately stored elements need
manual review. It does not move arbitrary polling control flow into callbacks.
`Changed` and `Submitted` polling can commit local bound values in the same
build pass, as described below.

## Element values and keys

```go
var element ui.Element
if element.Valid() {
    element.Focus()
}
```

Use `ui.Element{}` instead of assigning or returning `nil`. Custom parts
such as `ui.SelectParts[T]` are values containing checked elements too.

An element expires before the next build pass, including a rebuild within
the same frame. Generation validation rejects it even when its arena slot
has been reused. `Tester` and development builds panic with a message naming
the passes and recommending `ui.Handle`; production builds with
`mygo_noinspector` return empty query results or ignore stale mutations.
The absent zero value remains safe in either mode. `Valid` does not panic.

Assign keys before state initialization:

```go
ui.TextInput(c.Key("search"), &a.query).ReadOnly(a.readOnly)
ui.Checkbox(c.Key(todo.ID), &todo.Done, todo.Title)
parts := ui.SelectBase(c.Key("choice"), &a.choice)
```

`Element.Key` assigns a container's key before its children or local state
are built. Use `Context.Key` for stateful widgets, including
custom base controls. A key names the next outer control, and is consumed
before it initializes its state.

## Input and actions

A control writes the user's input through the pointer it binds before its
constructor returns, so bound values, local copies too, can be read
immediately; `Changed` and `Submitted` report it. Input follows the options
of the frame the user acted on: `Disabled`, `ReadOnly` and slider settings
set in a build govern the input of the frames after it.

```go
ui.Button(c, "Save").Disabled(a.saving).OnClick(a.save)
ui.TextInput(c.Key("query"), &a.query).OnChange(a.search)
ui.TextInput(c.Key("draft"), &a.draft).OnSubmit(a.send)
c.OnShortcut(ui.Cmd, ui.KeyS, a.save)
```

Click, shortcut, change and submit actions run after configuration and bound
input, before rebuilding. Handled input is consumed before another pass so
actions do not repeat. Polling methods remain available; prefer callbacks
when an action changes the collection being built. Keep I/O in workers and publish model results with
`Window.Update`.

Bind controls directly to persistent model fields when possible. A local
value recomputed on every build can be committed with `Changed` or
`Submitted` immediately, or with a callback after construction:

```go
viewed := a.isViewed(file)
if ui.Checkbox(c, &viewed, "Viewed").Changed() {
    a.setViewed(file, viewed)
}
```

The same rule applies to segmented controls whose selected value is derived
from several model fields. Review these bindings manually after running the
codemod; it cannot infer how to write a derived value back to your model.

## Persistent identity

Store `ui.Handle` instead of an element:

```go
type app struct {
    query string
    search ui.Handle
}

func (a *app) view(c *ui.Context) {
    ui.TextInput(c.Key("search"), &a.query).Bind(&a.search)
}

// On the UI thread, including inside Window.Update:
a.search.Focus()
```

Focus requests coalesce and wait while the control is hidden. Closing its
window cancels that window's request. `CancelFocus` cancels earlier.

`handle.Focused(c)` and `handle.FocusWithin(c)` read persistent identity,
including before the control is constructed. `c.Resolve(handle)` returns
only this pass's element. `handle.Bounds(c)` reads the committed control box
on the UI thread, including from an input callback. These are different queries: previous focus can
still be observed in the build that removes a control; committing that build
removes its actual focus.

A handle supports independent bindings in several windows. Queries take the
window's Context. Use `handle.Focus(c)` and `CancelFocus(c)` to select a
window; the no-argument Focus form requires at most one open binding. Before
the first binding, it waits for that first control. Give each window its own
widget state and focus field. `Ref`/`RequestFocus` are aliases for
`Handle`/`Focus`.

`ListState`, `ScrollState`, `GridState` and `Router` carry a Handle; other
controls can bind any app-owned handle. Use `state.Handle` for persistent focus and commands.

## Focus bound to app data

```go
type pane int
const (none pane = iota; files; diff)

ui.List(c, &a.list, len(a.files)).FocusBind(&a.pane, files).
    Rows(func(row ui.ListRow) { ui.Text(row.Context, a.files[row.Index].Name) })

// An action requests the diff pane, waiting while hidden:
a.pane = diff

// Actual focus can differ while that request waits:
focused := ui.FocusedValue(c, &a.pane)
```

`FocusBind` requires a pointer to a comparable field and a matching value.
Values are unique within that field in one window; reserve its zero value
for no focus. The field holds desired focus. User focus changes update it
when no request is waiting. Setting zero clears focus. `FocusedValue` reads
actual focus using committed identities, regardless of construction order.
A hidden binding keeps its desired request, while actual focus can be on
another control or absent. Use separate fields for separate windows.

## Lists and keyboard commands

```go
a.filesView.OnShortcut(c, ui.Cmd, ui.KeyK, a.openSelected)
ui.List(c.Key("files"), &a.list, len(a.files)).Bind(&a.filesView).Grow(1).
    ItemKey(func(i int) any { return a.files[i].ID }).
    Selection(&a.selection).
    Rows(func(row ui.ListRow) {
        text := ui.Text(row.Context, a.files[row.Index].Name)
        if row.Selected() && row.ListFocused() {
            text.TextColor(c.Theme().Accent)
        }
    })
```

A Handle's shortcut may be declared before Bind. It runs after construction
only if that window built an enabled control for the handle, so a hidden
control takes no command. `ListRow` supplies the shared Context, index,
selection and list focus. `List(c, state, n, func(i int))` also accepts a row
callback directly. Configure fluent lists before calling Rows.

## Persistent services and verification

Capture `c.Services()` for clipboard/URL callbacks and background redraws.
Services has weak window ownership and no build data. Clipboard and URL
methods run on the UI thread; Invalidate is safe from another goroutine.
Use `Window.Update` when publishing model changes.

`mygo vet` runs ordinary Go vet and type-aware checks for elements, parts,
and Context pointers stored in struct fields/package variables or captured
by/passed to goroutines. It follows imports, type aliases and inferred
variables; Handle, Services and view callback signatures are allowed.
These checks help enforce build lifetimes; they do not prove all lifetimes
or goroutine safety. Runtime generation checks remain necessary.

Exercise controls disappearing and returning, pending focus, list reordering,
text editing/IME, disabled and read-only settings, and command routing. Run
normal tests and inspect the app. See [Performance](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/performance.md) for
measured costs and reproduction commands.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/motion.md

# Motion

<!-- preview motion 220 -->

An element animates values for you: you give the target, it returns the
value to show in this frame, and draws frames until the value gets there.
The view says where things are; the animation finds the way:

```go
card := ui.Box(c).Size(120, 80).Radius(12).Background(t.Accent)
target := float32(0)
if app.open {
	target = 200
}
card.Translate(card.AnimateTo("x", target, ui.Snappy), 0)
```

The key (`"x"`) tells apart the values of one element, which needs the same
ID from frame to frame: a `Key`, or the same place among its siblings. A
value starts at its first target. Use the value in any way: a transform
(see [Transforms](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/transforms.md)), a size, an opacity, a color mix, or what
a `Draw` paints.

## Animations

An `Animation` says how a value goes to a new target:

* **Springs**, the zero `Animation` and the presets `ui.Smooth` (no
  bounce), `ui.Snappy` (a little) and `ui.Bouncy` (a visible one). A
  spring keeps its velocity when its target changes on the way: clicked
  again mid-flight, the card above turns around smoothly instead of
  stopping dead.
* **Curves**: a `Duration` and an `Ease` (`ui.EaseOut` when nil), as
  `ui.Animation{Duration: 150 * time.Millisecond, Ease: ui.EaseInOut}`.
  `Animate(key, target, d)` and `AnimateWith(key, target, d, ease)` are
  short for them.

A spring's `SpringOptions` describe it as one perceives it, with a
`Duration` (500 ms when zero), about how long it takes to arrive, and a
`Bounce`, from 0, arriving without overshooting, toward 1; negative values
arrive more slowly still. These are SwiftUI's and Motion's parameters.
`Stiffness`, `Damping` and `Mass` describe it physically instead:

```go
gentle := ui.Animation{Spring: ui.SpringOptions{Duration: 700 * time.Millisecond, Bounce: 0.1}}
stiff := ui.Animation{Spring: ui.SpringOptions{Stiffness: 400, Damping: 30}}
x := card.AnimateTo("x", target, gentle)
```

`Spring(key, target, options)` is short for `AnimateTo` with a spring.
Springs are solved exactly rather than stepped, so a slow frame does not
change their path. A value can change its kind of animation on the way: a
spring taking over a curve keeps the curve's velocity.

`Easing` functions are `ui.Linear`, `ui.EaseIn`, `ui.EaseOut`,
`ui.EaseInOut`, `ui.Bounce(e)`, CSS's `ui.CubicBezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)`, or
any `func(t float32) float32`.

`AnimateColor(key, target, a)` animates a color the same way, mixed with
premultiplied alpha, so that a color fading in from transparent keeps its
hue:

```go
row.Background(row.AnimateColor("bg", bg, ui.Animation{Duration: 120 * time.Millisecond}))
```

## Poses that only paint

The values above are read by the view, so every frame that moves runs it.
`AnimatePose` moves an element instead: it translates, scales, turns and
fades it, after its own transform, and the frames that move it only paint,
without running the view, as Core Animation and the Web Animations API run
transforms and opacity. It is the cheapest motion there is, which keeps a
large view smooth:

```go
lift := ui.Pose{}
if card.Hovered() {
	lift = ui.Pose{Y: -4, Scale: 1.02}
}
card.AnimatePose(lift, ui.Snappy)
```

A `Pose` moves by `X` and `Y`, scales by `Scale` (0 keeps the size),
turns by `Rotate` degrees, and fades by `Fade`, from 0, opaque, to 1, gone.
The pointer, carets and overlays follow the element as it moves, and
`Transitioning()` reports whether its pose was moving.

Poses nest: each acts after those of the elements around it, so an
element inside another adds its own motion, along its own curve. In the
[confetti example](https://github.com/egoist/mygo/tree/main/examples/confetti), a burst falls and fades, each
piece in it bursts out along a curve that slows down, and spins inside:
hundreds of pieces fly without building the view again. Each element
posed still costs every frame that paints it, so share a pose among the
elements that move alike, as the burst's fall, rather than giving each
its own.

## Delays and staggering

`Delay` keeps the value going as it was for a while after its target
changes. Delays growing with the index stagger a list:

```go
for i, it := range app.items {
	row := ui.Row(c.Key(it.ID))
	a := ui.Snappy
	a.Delay = time.Duration(i) * 30 * time.Millisecond
	row.Opacity(row.AnimateTo("shown", 1, a))
}
```

## Gestures

`Draggable` lets the pointer move an element and throw it, as motion.dev's
`drag` does: the element follows the pointer, and once let go, the
pointer's velocity carries it to where it comes to rest, with a spring:

```go
card := ui.Box(c).Size(90, 60).Radius(10).Background(t.Accent)
card.Draggable(&app.card, ui.DraggableOptions{
	Axis:   ui.Horizontal,
	Bounds: &ui.Rect{W: 200},
	Snap:   ui.Nearest(ui.Point{}, ui.Point{X: 200}),
})
```

`app.card` is a `ui.Point`, the element's offset from its place in the
layout. As the pointer drags the element, it follows the pointer; once the
pointer lets go, it is where the element comes to rest; and setting it
moves the element there, as a button turning a page does. A nil offset is
kept in the element. The options say how it moves:

* **`Axis`**, `ui.Horizontal` or `ui.Vertical`, is the direction it moves
  in; both when zero.
* **`Bounds`** hold the offset within a rectangle at rest, from `X` to
  `X+W` and from `Y` to `Y+H`. The pointer pulls the element past them less
  and less far, as iOS holds content pulled past its edges, and it springs
  back within them once let go. `Rigid` stops it at them.
* **`Snap`** chooses where it comes to rest, from where the throw would
  carry it (`ui.Project`, held within the bounds), so that a flick goes
  on to the next page or height: `ui.Nearest(points...)` chooses the
  nearest of points. A `Snap` returning its point lets the
  element glide where the throw carries it. Without `Snap`, it rests where
  the pointer lets it go, as an item placed on a canvas.
* **`Animation`** is how it goes to rest, and to an offset the app sets:
  `ui.Smooth` when zero. A spring starts at the pointer's velocity.

The pointer drags the element once it moved a few DIPs, and that press is
no click; a press on the element as it moves catches it. The element moves
after its own transform and its pose, along its parent's axes, so it
stays under the pointer as it scales or turns, and it goes to rest in
frames that only paint, without building the view, as `AnimatePose`
moves it. `Dragging()` reports that the pointer drags it, to lift it as
it does:

```go
lift := ui.Pose{}
if card.Dragging() {
	lift = ui.Pose{Scale: 1.05}
}
card.AnimatePose(lift, ui.Snappy)
```

`Transitioning()` is false once it is at rest, for the view to go on, as
removing a row swiped away:

```go
for i := range app.rows {
	r := &app.rows[i]
	row := ui.Row(c).Key(r.ID)
	row.Draggable(&r.swipe, ui.DraggableOptions{
		Axis: ui.Horizontal,
		Snap: func(p ui.Point) ui.Point {
			if p.X < -160 {
				return ui.Point{X: -400} // away to the left
			}
			return ui.Point{}
		},
	})
	if r.swipe.X == -400 && !row.Transitioning() {
		app.remove(r.ID)
	}
}
```

`DragOffset()` returns where the element shows in this frame, following
the pointer or on its way to rest, for what follows it, as a backdrop
fading as a sheet goes down. Reading it builds the view in every frame
the element moves in, as `AnimateTo` does; call it after `Draggable`:

```go
backdrop := ui.Box(c).Absolute().Fill().Background(ui.RGBA(0, 0, 0, 0.4))
sheet := ui.Column(c).Draggable(&app.sheet, ui.DraggableOptions{
	Axis:   ui.Vertical,
	Bounds: &ui.Rect{H: 400},
	Snap:   ui.Nearest(ui.Point{}, ui.Point{Y: 400}),
})
backdrop.Opacity(1 - sheet.DragOffset().Y/400)
```

While the desktop asks for less motion, the element follows the pointer,
and goes to rest at once.

### By hand

For a value other than an offset that follows the pointer, as the angle
of a dial, build the gesture from smaller pieces. `Jump` sets a value
at once, following the pointer, and keeps track of how fast it moves; the
spring that takes over when the pointer lets go starts at that speed.
`DragEnded` reports the pointer's velocity as it let go, which
`SpringOptions.Velocity` hands to the spring:

```go
dial := ui.Box(c).Size(80, 80)
var turn float32
if dx, _, ok := dial.Dragged(); ok {
	app.turn += dx
	turn = dial.Jump("turn", app.turn)
} else {
	a := ui.Snappy
	if vx, _, ok := dial.DragEnded(); ok {
		// Where the throw would carry it decides the notch it lands on.
		app.turn = float32(math.Round(float64(ui.Project(app.turn, vx)/45))) * 45
		a.Spring.Velocity = vx
	}
	turn = dial.AnimateTo("turn", app.turn, a)
}
dial.Transform(ui.Rotation(turn))
```

`DragVelocity` is the pointer's velocity while it presses, in DIPs per
second along the element's axes, zero once it rests a moment. `Velocity(key)`
is the velocity of an animated value. A click, which does not move, ends no
drag.

`ui.Project(value, velocity)` is where a fling would carry a value as
iOS's scroll views slow down, to choose where it lands, as a page of a
pager. `ui.Rubberband(value, lo, hi, dimension)` holds a value dragged past
lo or hi as iOS holds content pulled past its edges, going less and less
far:

```go
if _, dy, ok := sheet.Dragged(); ok {
	app.y += dy
	y = sheet.Jump("y", ui.Rubberband(app.y, 0, 400, 600))
}
```

## When it is done

`Settled(key)` reports whether a value rests at its target, and
`Arrived(key)` is true in the one frame in which it came to rest, for the
view to go on, as removing what faded out:

```go
toast.Opacity(toast.AnimateTo("fade", 0, ui.Animation{Duration: 200 * time.Millisecond}))
if toast.Arrived("fade") {
	app.dismiss(toast)
}
```

## Without animation

`c.DisableAnimations()` makes the values, transitions, poses and router
pages of the frame go to their targets at once, as SwiftUI's
disablesAnimations: for a change that should not show as motion, as
restoring a window's state or jumping to a search result. Call it before
building what changes. `Keyframes` and timelines play on their own rather
than towards a target, and go on as they were; seek a timeline to jump it.

## Keyframes

`Keyframes` plays timed values, each segment along the `Ease` of the frame
it arrives at, and holds the last:

```go
tile := ui.Box(c).Key("tile").Size(80, 50)
x := tile.Keyframes("x", []ui.Keyframe{
	{Value: 0},
	{At: 200 * time.Millisecond, Value: 100, Ease: ui.EaseOut},
	{At: 700 * time.Millisecond, Value: 40},
	{At: time.Second, Value: 0, Ease: ui.EaseInOut},
}, ui.KeyframeOptions{Run: app.shakes})
tile.Translate(x, 0)
```

The first time must be zero and later times must increase. Change `Run` to
play the sequence again, or a changed one: interrupted, it starts from the
value shown rather than jumping to its first, the first time through.
`Repeat` is how many more times it plays after the first, `RepeatForever`
for as long as it is built, with `Alternate` playing every other time
backward; `Delay` holds the first value for a while before it plays, and
`RepeatDelay` the value it got to between plays.

## Timelines

A `Timeline` plays several tweens along one playhead, so motion that belongs
together is arranged, controlled and tested together: a card arriving while
its title fades in, rows following one another, a small bounce after the
card lands. `AnimateTo` moves one value of one element towards a target, and
`Keyframes` plays one value along timed stops; a timeline coordinates many
such values, each tween of its own, around one clock.

An element keeps a timeline under a key, as it keeps `Keyframes`: build it
in the view, as everything else, and give each tween the value it shows
this frame:

```go
card := ui.Column(c)
tl := card.Timeline("intro", ui.TimelineOptions{Run: app.opened})
x := tl.Tween(ui.Tween{From: -200, To: 0, Duration: 400 * time.Millisecond})
fade := tl.Tween(ui.Tween{From: 0, To: 1, Duration: 300 * time.Millisecond},
	ui.AfterPrevious(-150*time.Millisecond))
card.Translate(x, 0).Opacity(fade)
```

A tween eases out (`EaseOut`) unless its `Ease` says otherwise, as an
`Animation` does. A tween with no placement follows the one before it at
once, so here the second would start at 400ms; placements put it
elsewhere, as GSAP's position parameter does:

| Placement                               | Starts the tween                                                                                             |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `AfterPrevious(50*time.Millisecond)`    | 50ms after the one before it ends; a negative offset overlaps it, as `-150ms` above starts the fade at 250ms |
| `WithPrevious(0)`                       | where the one before it starts, to move along with it, or an offset after that                               |
| `AtLabel("rows", 100*time.Millisecond)` | 100ms after a label                                                                                          |
| `AtTime(500*time.Millisecond)`          | at a time of the timeline                                                                                    |

Nothing starts before the timeline does: a placement before its start is
at its start.

### Labels and stagger

`Label` marks a time of the timeline for tweens to start at, and an offset
from it staggers them by index:

```go
tl := list.Timeline("rows", ui.TimelineOptions{Run: app.shown})
tl.Label("rows", ui.AtTime(300*time.Millisecond))
for i := range app.rows {
	app.rows[i] = tl.Tween(ui.Tween{From: 0, To: 1, Duration: 200 * time.Millisecond},
		ui.AtLabel("rows", time.Duration(i)*40*time.Millisecond))
}
for i, shown := range app.rows {
	rows[i].Opacity(shown).Translate(0, (1-shown)*12)
}
```

### Playing it

`Duration` is the end of the last tween, `Time` where the playhead is, and
`Progress` how far along it is, from 0 to 1, for a scrubber. `Paused` holds
the playhead where it is: time a paused timeline spends is not time it
played, so letting a pause go plays on from where it held, however long the
pause was. `Reverse` plays it backward from where the playhead is to its
start, as a panel that closes the way it opened (`Reverse: !app.open`), and
a timeline played over while reversed plays from its end. `Seek` and
`Progress` hold it at a time or a part of the timeline for as long as they
are given, going on from there when they are not; give one of them at
most. What the options say takes
effect in the frame it is said in, so a button that pauses or plays the
timeline again shows in the frame it was clicked in:

```go
o := ui.TimelineOptions{Run: app.run, Paused: app.paused, Reverse: app.reverse}
if app.scrubbing {
	o.Progress = &app.scrub
}
tl := card.Timeline("intro", o)
```

`Repeat` is how many more times the timeline plays after the first, as
`KeyframeOptions.Repeat` is, `RepeatForever` for as long as the view builds
it, with `Alternate` playing every other time backward; `Delay` holds the
timeline at its first value for a while before it plays, and `RepeatDelay`
the value it got to between plays. `Settled` reports that it rests, at
its end or, in reverse, at its start, and `Arrived` is true in the one frame
in which it came to rest, as `Settled(key)` and `Arrived(key)` are for a
value.

Change `Run` to play the timeline again, or a changed one. Building it
without changing `Run` keeps the playhead where it is, so a view may
rearrange its tweens from frame to frame: the timeline plays the ones it
arranged this frame. Arranging a longer one goes on from where the playhead
is, and it is not `Settled` until the timeline it arranged has played. A
timeline goes with its element's state when the view stops building the
element. An element asks for each of its timelines once per build, and the
`*Timeline` it returns is good while the view builds that frame.

While the desktop asks for less motion, a timeline that would play is at
once where it would come to rest, every tween at its `To`, or at its `From`
when it plays back to its start, as values, poses and `Keyframes` are, and
it asks for no frame. What the view does with the playhead itself still
works, as a drag still moves a `Draggable` element: `Seek` and `Progress`
put it where a scrubber asks, and `Paused` holds it there.
`DisableAnimations` does not change a timeline, which plays on its own as
`Keyframes` do; `Seek` jumps it. A timeline draws frames only while it
plays, timed by `c.Now()`.

## Scrolling

`InView()` reports whether some of an element showed in the frame before,
within the scroll containers around it, to bring it in as it scrolls into
view. A `ScrollState` (see [Scrolling](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/scroll.md)) gives how far its
container scrolled, for effects that follow the scrolling:

```go
card := ui.Box(c).Key(it.ID).Height(120)
shown := float32(0)
if card.InView() {
	shown = 1
}
card.Opacity(card.AnimateTo("shown", shown, ui.Smooth))

header.Opacity(1 - min(app.scroll.Y/80, 1)) // fades as the page scrolls
```

`ScrollState.ScrollTo(x, y, animation)` scrolls a container smoothly (see
[Scrolling](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/scroll.md)).

## Content that changes

`ContentTransition` animates an element's content as it changes: the text
of a `Text`, the icon of an `Icon`, the picture of an `Image`. By default
the old content fades out as the new fades in, and an icon shrinks away as
the new one grows in. `Numeric` rolls the characters of a line of text that
change, as a counter's digits, those that stay staying: up, or with `Down`
down, as SwiftUI's numericText:

```go
ui.Text(c, strconv.Itoa(app.count)).FontSize(32).Bold().
	ContentTransition(ui.ContentTransition{Numeric: true, Down: app.decreased})
ui.Icon(c, playOrPause).ContentTransition(ui.ContentTransition{})
```

Content transitions run in frames that only paint. While the desktop asks
for less motion, content fades without moving.

## Loops and your own motion

`Loop` returns the progress of an animation that starts over every period,
for spinners and pulses (see [Drawing and animation](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/drawing.md#animation)).
To animate otherwise, compute from `c.Now()` and call `c.AnimationFrame()`
in every frame that moves.

## Less motion and frames

When the desktop asks for less motion (`c.Preferences().ReduceMotion`),
values and poses go to their targets at once and sequences end at their
last value. What changes without moving still changes smoothly: colors
(`AnimateColor`), a pose's `Fade`, content fading across, and
[transitions](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/transitions.md)' colors and fades. `Loop` goes on, as the
system's spinners do.

Animations draw frames only while something moves, at the display's rate,
and none while the window is out of sight (below). Frames moving values
the view reads run the view; poses, content transitions, and drawings that
animate from their `Draw` only paint.

## Out of sight

While nothing of a window shows (on macOS: hidden, minimized, on another
Space, or entirely covered by other windows; in a browser: a tab in the
background), MyGo draws no frames for it, as browsers draw nothing for
pages out of sight and as Apple asks of Mac apps. The view does not run,
`Draw` is not called, and the frames `After` and `Painter.After` ask for
wait. As soon as some of the window shows, it draws once, with everything
that changed meanwhile; until then the screen shows its last frame, for
about a refresh. A frame still builds after input (keys typed into a key
window another app's window covers), when assistive technology turns on,
and for `Window.CapturePage`, so that a capture shows the window as it is
now. Windows and Linux do not tell MyGo when a window is out of sight, so
there it draws as it always did.

What this means for motion:

* **What MyGo animates goes on from where the time puts it.** A spring,
  an `Animate` on its way, a `Loop`, keyframes and timelines running when
  the window went out of sight are further along, or done, when it shows.
* **A target that changed out of sight animates when the window shows.**
  The view first sees the new target then, so the value moves to it from
  where it was, as a CSS transition does for a change made in a hidden
  tab.
* **Compute your own motion from the time, not from frames.** A start
  time taken in the first frame that draws something, or a count of
  frames, starts over when the window shows, and plays what happened
  meanwhile as if it just began. Take the time from when the state
  changed, in the code that changes it, and the view shows a change made
  out of sight as done:

```go
// counter eases from one value to the next over 400 ms, by the clock.
type counter struct {
	from, to float32
	changed  time.Time
}

const ease = 400 * time.Millisecond

// at returns the value shown at t.
func (n counter) at(t time.Time) float32 {
	p := min(float32(t.Sub(n.changed))/float32(ease), 1)
	return n.from + (n.to-n.from)*ui.EaseOut(p)
}

// Where the count changes, outside the view:
now := time.Now()
app.count = counter{from: app.count.at(now), to: float32(n), changed: now}
win.Update(func() {})

// In the view:
value := app.count.at(c.Now())
if c.Now().Sub(app.count.changed) < ease {
	c.AnimationFrame()
}
```

* **Keep work out of the view.** Polling, saving, or starting jobs from
  the view, from `After` or from a `Draw` waits while the window is out of
  sight. Run such work from the app (a goroutine or a `time.Ticker`) and
  show what it does with `Window.Update`.

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/navigation.md

# Pages and navigation

A `ui.Router` keeps the history of the pages of a window, or of a part of
one, as a browser does for a tab. A page is a path, as `/notes/42`, which
`View` matches to build the page shown, a `switch` over patterns whose
`{name}` takes one part of the path and `{name...}` the rest.

The router is part of your app's state: make it once, with the page to
show first, and keep it in a field. The view, which runs for every frame,
builds the page it shows:

```go
// notesApp is the app's state.
type notesApp struct {
	router *ui.Router
	// … the notes and the files
}

func main() {
	app := &notesApp{router: ui.NewRouter("/notes")}
	mygo.App.WhenReady(func() {
		mygo.NewWindow(mygo.WindowOptions{Title: "Notes", Content: ui.View(app.view)})
	})
	if err := mygo.App.Run(); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

func (app *notesApp) view(c *ui.Context) {
	ui.Row(c).Fill().AlignItems(ui.Stretch).Children(func() {
		app.sidebar(c) // stays as the pages change, see below
		app.router.View(c, func(r *ui.Route) {
			switch {
			case r.Match("/notes"):
				r.Title("Notes")
				app.notes(c)
			case r.Match("/notes/{id}"):
				r.Title("Note")
				app.note(c, r.Param("id"))
			case r.Match("/files/{path...}"):
				app.files(c, r.Param("path"))
			default:
				ui.Text(c, "Not found")
			}
		})
	})
}
```

`app.notes`, `app.note` and `app.files` are methods of `notesApp` that
build those pages, as `view` builds the window.

## Going to pages

`Push` goes to a page, after the page shown, `Replace` shows one in its
place, and `Back`, `Forward` and `Go` move through the history; paths
relative to the page shown resolve as links in a web page do, so
`Push("?tab=info")` changes the query and `Push("edit")` goes to a sibling.
A [link](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/link.md) to a path in a page goes there in its router, and
choosing an item of a [sidebar](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/sidebar.md) pushes its page, as the sidebar
of the app above does:

```go
func (app *notesApp) sidebar(c *ui.Context) {
	page := app.router.Path()
	ui.Sidebar(c, &page, func() {
		ui.SidebarItem(c, "/notes", nil, "Notes")
		ui.SidebarItem(c, "/files", nil, "Files")
	}).Width(220).OnChange(func() {
		app.router.Push(page)
	})
}

// In a page:
ui.Link(c, "Open note", "/notes/42")
```

`Path`, `Query` and `Location` read the page shown; `Location` with its
query, which `NewRouter` takes to show it again when the app starts. A deep
link (`mygo.App.OnOpenURL`) pushes its page.

## Back and forward

Users go back and forward as in browsers and Finder: Cmd+\[ and Cmd+] on
macOS, Alt+Left and Alt+Right on Linux and Windows, the back and forward
buttons of a mouse and the keys of keyboards that have them, swiping
between pages on a touchpad on macOS, and the
[back and forward buttons](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/history-buttons.md), which a toolbar holds, and
whose right click lists the pages to go back or forward to, by their
titles. The keys go to the router holding the keyboard focus, else to the
first of the window.

In a [browser](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/browsers.md), the first router a window shows follows the
tab's history, in the URL's fragment (`#/notes/42`): going to a page adds
an entry to the browser's history, its back and forward buttons go through
the router's pages, and a URL with a fragment, opened or reloaded, shows
its page. After a reload, the router learns the pages before and after
the one shown as the browser goes to them. An app in a frame of another
page leaves the tab's history alone.

## Layouts

Anything built around `View`, as a sidebar or a toolbar, stays as pages
change. A page can also be a layout around the pages of the rest of its
path, as a page of settings with a list of its sections beside the section
shown: `r.View` on its route builds them, matching what the pattern's
`{name...}` took. The layout stays as they change, keeping its state, and
they slide or fade in its place; `Param` reads the layout's wildcards too.
A page of settings is another case of the `switch` in the view above:

```go
case r.Match("/settings/{section...}"):
	ui.Row(c).Grow(1).Children(func() {
		app.sectionList(c) // pushes "/settings/general", "/settings/fonts"
		r.View(c, func(r *ui.Route) {
			switch {
			case r.Match("/general"):
				r.Title("General")
				app.general(c)
			case r.Match("/fonts"):
				r.Title("Fonts")
				app.fonts(c)
			}
		})
	})
```

A second `Router` inside a page, in a field of its own, is a history of its
own, as the detail of a split view going deeper while the list beside it
stays.

## Pages keep their state

A page keeps the state of its elements while it is in the history, ten
pages either way: going back to one finds it scrolled where it was, with
its text and the keyboard focus where they were. A path with another query
is the same page, in another entry of the history, keeping its state, as a
page whose tabs or search are in its query.

## The focus and screen readers

Going to a page moves the keyboard focus into it, to the element that had
it there, else to the page itself, which Tab goes into; screen readers read
the page's `Title`. With the focus outside the page that changes, as in a
sidebar or a layout's list choosing the pages, it stays there, and screen
readers hear the title of the page.

## Transitions

A page deeper in the paths, as `/notes/42` after `/notes`, slides in from
the right over the page it leaves, and back up from the left; others fade
in. With less motion asked of the desktop, all fade, and
`router.Transition = ui.TransitionNone` shows them at once. The page going
away takes neither the pointer nor the keyboard as it slides.

`router.Animation` sets how pages move, as a spring or a curve (see
[Motion](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/motion.md)), in place of easing out over 250 ms as they slide and
150 ms as they fade:

```go
router.Animation = &ui.Snappy
```

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/number-input.md

# Number input

<!-- preview number-input 160 -->

`ui.NumberInput` creates a text input editing a `*float64` as a number
between two bounds, which Up and Down, and the buttons beside it, change by
a step. What is typed applies as soon as it is a number in range, and shows
rounded to the decimals of the step once the input loses the focus.
`Changed` reports a new value.

```go
ui.NumberInput(c, &app.copies, 1, 99, 1).Label("Copies")
ui.NumberInput(c, &app.opacity, 0, 1, 0.05).Label("Opacity")
```

For a value the user only steps, use a [stepper](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/stepper.md); for one
chosen roughly, a [slider](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/slider.md).

## Accessibility

Assistive technology sees a spin button of the value, named by its `Label`
or its [field](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/form.md), which it increments and decrements by the step.

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/outline.md

# Outline

<!-- preview outline 320 -->

`ui.Outline` shows a tree of items, as AppKit's outline view and Finder's
list view: items at the top, and below each item open its children,
indented, with an arrow that opens and closes it. The app gives the items at
the top and `children`, which returns an item's, nil for one without any;
the outline builds only the rows in view, as a [list](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/list.md) does, so
trees of any size are as fast as small ones.

```go
type fileTree struct {
	children map[string][]string // the paths in each directory
	files    ui.OutlineState[string]
	row      int
}

func (app *fileTree) view(c *ui.Context) {
	app.files.List.Selected = &app.row
	ui.Outline(c, &app.files, []string{"/"}, func(dir string) []string {
		return app.children[dir] // nil for a file
	}, func(path string) {
		ui.Text(c, filepath.Base(path))
	}).Grow(1)
	chosen := app.files.Item(app.row)
	// …
}
```

## Outline state

Its state, an `OutlineState`, holds the rows' `ListState`, which chooses
rows as a list's does (`Selected`, `Selection`), and the items `Open`, a
`Selection` of the items showing their children. The rows' keys are the
items, so their choice and state follow them as items open and close above
them. `Rows`, `Item` and `Depth` read the rows shown. `Indent` is the width
each level adds before a row's arrow, the theme's `Space(4)` when zero; it
must not be negative.

## Opening and closing

* A click on an item's arrow opens or closes it; Option-click (Alt-click)
  opens or closes all inside it too.
* While the outline has the focus, Right opens the item chosen or goes to
  its first child, and Left closes it or goes to its parent; with Option on
  macOS and Shift elsewhere, as in GTK, they open and close all inside.
* Closing an item whose child was chosen chooses the item.

## In columns

`ui.OutlineTable` is the same in a [table](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/table.md)'s columns, the first of
which shows the arrows, indented as the items are deep: the columns are a
table's, which the user sorts, resizes and moves.

```go
ui.OutlineTable(c, &app.files, cols, roots, children, func(path string, col int) {
	switch col {
	case 0:
		ui.Text(c, filepath.Base(path)).SingleLine()
	case 1:
		ui.Text(c, app.size(path))
	}
})
```

## Accessibility

Assistive technology sees a tree, or a table with rows that open and close,
whose rows say their level, whether they open, and whether they are open,
and which of all the rows they are; it opens and closes them as the arrows
do.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/overlays.md

# Overlays

Overlays show above the window's content: [dialogs](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/dialog.md) over the
dimmed window, [alert dialogs](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/alert-dialog.md), [popovers](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/popover.md)
below an element, the popups of [selects](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/select.md) and
[comboboxes](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/combobox.md), [tooltips](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/tooltip.md) and [toasts](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/toast.md).
They share how they treat the keyboard and what is behind them.

```go
more := ui.Button(c, "More ▾")
if more.Clicked() {
	app.menu = !app.menu
}
ui.Popover(c, more, &app.menu, func() {
	if ui.Button(c, "Rename").Clicked() {
		app.menu, app.renaming = false, true
	}
})
ui.Modal(c, &app.renaming, func() {
	ui.Text(c, "Rename").Bold()
	if ui.TextInput(c, &app.name).AutoFocus().Submitted() {
		app.renaming = false
	}
})
```

## The keyboard

A dialog keeps the keyboard: it takes the focus as it opens, on its first
element that takes it unless one in it asked for it (`AutoFocus`), Tab goes
round its elements, and the window's shortcuts built outside it wait, as
what is behind it is inert, which screen readers do not see either. A
popover's elements follow its anchor as Tab moves.

Escape closes the overlay on top, a select's popup before the dialog it is
in, unless the focused element takes it, as a terminal does; and an
overlay that closes with the focus in it gives the focus back to the
element that had it as it opened, its button say.

A press outside a popover closes it and goes on to what is under the
pointer, as with the web's popovers: a click on another button closes the
popover and presses the button. A select's popup takes the press, as the
system's pop-up menus do, and a dialog's backdrop closes it.

## Your own overlays

`ui.Overlay` builds elements above everything else, placed with `Absolute`
in DIPs of the window:

```go
ui.Overlay(c, func() {
	ui.Text(c, "Offline").Absolute().Top(12).Right(12).
		Padding(4, 10).Radius(999).Background(t.Danger).TextColor(t.AccentText)
})
```

`PopoverBase` and `DialogBase` are a popover and a dialog without a look,
for overlays of your own design: see [custom widgets](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/custom-widgets.md).
Overlays that neither fits, as a drawer, a hover card or a menu bar's
menus, are built from what those are made of:

* `AttachTo(target, at, self)` places an element beside another, wherever
  that one is: its point `self` on the point `at` of the target, as
  `AttachTo(button, ui.AnchorBottomLeft, ui.AnchorTopLeft)` below a button.
  Where it would leave the window, it goes to the other side, or the other
  way along the target, then moves into the window; one that scrolls
  vertically is no taller than the room on the target's larger side, and
  scrolls. Its margins keep it apart from the target. It is the target's popover: its elements follow
  the target as Tab moves.
* `PressedOutside` reports a press outside an element, its target and the
  popovers of what is inside it, as a popover closes for.
* `OverlayShortcut` takes the keys the focused element and those around it
  leave, wherever the focus is, the overlay built last first, as Escape
  closing the one on top.
* `Modal` makes an element a dialog's backdrop: the focus moves into it
  and stays there, the window's shortcuts outside it wait, and screen
  readers see only it and what is above it.

Each element built at the top of `ui.Overlay` gives the focus back to the
element that had it as it came, when it goes with the focus in it. A
drawer on the right, closing with Escape or a click on its backdrop:

```go
if app.drawer {
	ui.Overlay(c, func() {
		back := ui.Row(c).Absolute().Left(0).Top(0).Right(0).Bottom(0).Justify(ui.End).
			Background(ui.RGBA(0, 0, 0, 0.3)).Modal()
		back.Children(func() {
			panel := ui.Column(c).Width(320).FillHeight().Padding(16).Background(t.Background).
				Role(ui.RoleDialog).Label("Filters").Children(app.filters)
			if panel.PressedOutside() || back.OverlayShortcut(0, ui.KeyEscape) {
				app.drawer = false
			}
		})
	})
}
```

Native [dialogs](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/native.md#dialogs) work too: call them from a goroutine,
so that the view does not wait for them.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/performance.md

# Native UI performance

These measurements cover steady frames rendered on the CPU with `ui.Tester`.
They were taken on October 8, 2026 on Apple M5, macOS arm64, Go 1.27.1, with
`CGO_ENABLED=0 GOMAXPROCS=1`. Each timing is the median of six sequential
300 ms samples after warming the view.

| Fixture                                    | Time per frame | Allocations per frame | Allocated bytes per frame |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------: | --------------------: | ------------------------: |
| 1,000 static labels                        |         397 µs |                     0 |                         0 |
| Visible rows of a million-row list         |        14.5 µs |                    20 |                       176 |
| Diff view with no changes                  |         389 µs |                     2 |                        72 |
| A 50 KB Markdown reply, shown whole        |         1.3 ms |                   353 |                    15,894 |
| The same reply streaming, 16 bytes a frame |         0.8 ms |                   350 |                    35,946 |

The Markdown rows, `BenchmarkViewSteady` and `BenchmarkViewStream` of
`ui/markdown`, were taken on October 14, 2026, on a busier machine; see
[Markdown](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/markdown.md#performance) for the parser's own costs.

Element handles validate their owner, arena slot and build generation.
Static label handles do not allocate. Input bindings, action queues and
persistent identity bindings reuse storage once warmed. Composite controls
can allocate callback closures; these fixtures do not cover every widget
or interaction.

The label and list fixtures use the public API. The diff fixture uses the
private renderer API and measures its steady-frame allocation floor.

## Retained memory

A warmed view containing 1,000 labels retained approximately **2.50 MB of
Go heap**, measured over three samples. The measurement warms fonts and
rendering, releases a warm view, forces collection, then measures a second
retained view after ten frames and another collection.

This includes the headless rendering host. It does not measure native window
process memory or GPU resources.

## Measurement scope

Timing depends on the machine, rendering backend, content and activity in
other processes. Small timing differences should be rechecked on several
machines; allocation counts are more stable. These results describe steady
frames and do not compare MyGo with another GUI framework.

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/popover.md

# Popover

<!-- preview popover 240 -->

`ui.Popover` shows a panel its function builds below an element, its
anchor, while a `*bool` is true; pressing outside it or Escape sets it to
false. The press goes on to what is under the pointer, as with the web's
popovers: a click on another button closes the popover and presses the
button, and one on the anchor closes it, as the anchor toggles it. Where
there is no room below the anchor, the panel shows above it, and it
follows the anchor as the window scrolls.

```go
more := ui.Button(c, "More ▾")
if more.Clicked() {
	app.menu = !app.menu
}
ui.Popover(c, more, &app.menu, func() {
	if ui.Button(c, "Rename").Clicked() {
		app.menu, app.renaming = false, true
	}
	if ui.Button(c, "Duplicate").Clicked() {
		app.menu = false
		app.duplicate()
	}
})
```

`Dismissed` reports the frame a press outside or Escape closed the popover;
one that must stay open sets the `*bool` back to true then.

A popover's elements follow its anchor as Tab moves, and as it closes with
the focus in it, it gives the focus back to the element that had it. See
[overlays](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/overlays.md).

For a menu of the system's, use a [menu button](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/menu-button.md); for a tip,
a [tooltip](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/tooltip.md). A popover shows in its window: one that must
extend beyond the window's edges shows in a [flyout](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/windows.md#flyouts),
a window of its own placed next to the anchor.

## Without a look

`ui.PopoverBase` is a popover without a look: its function styles the panel
and builds its content. A top margin keeps the panel apart from the anchor,
on either side:

```go
ui.PopoverBase(c, anchor, &app.open, func(panel ui.Element) {
	panel.Margin(6, 0, 0, 0).Padding(8).Radius(12).Background(t.Background).Shadow(0, 8, 24, 0, ui.RGBA(0, 0, 0, 0.2))
	app.filters(c)
})
```

The panel goes elsewhere with `AttachTo`: to the right of the anchor, its
middles lined up, and to the left where there is no room on the right:

```go
ui.PopoverBase(c, anchor, &app.open, func(panel ui.Element) {
	panel.AttachTo(anchor, ui.AnchorRight, ui.AnchorLeft).Margin(0, 0, 0, 6)
	app.details(c)
})
```

Popovers of your own, as a hover card, are built in an overlay with
`AttachTo` and `PressedOutside`: see [overlays](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/overlays.md#your-own-overlays).

See [custom widgets](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/custom-widgets.md).

## Accessibility

Assistive technology sees the panel as a popup after its anchor.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/progress.md

# Progress bar

<!-- preview progress 180 -->

`ui.Progress` creates a progress bar filled to a value between 0 and 1; a
negative value shows activity of unknown length, a segment sliding across.

```go
ui.Progress(c, float64(app.done)/float64(app.total)).Label("Uploading")
ui.Progress(c, -1).Label("Connecting")
```

`Reverse` fills it from the right, for interfaces laid out from right to
left. It stretches across its column; give it a `Width` in a row.

A bar of unknown length moves only while it is in view, and costs only its
painting: the window paints the last frame again at the display's rate,
without running the view.

For a spinning indicator that takes less room, use a
[spinner](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/spinner.md); for a level that is no progress, as a disk's use, a
[meter](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/meter.md).

## Accessibility

Assistive technology sees a progress indicator of the value, or of unknown
length, named by its `Label`.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/radio.md

# Radio

<!-- preview radio 160 -->

`ui.Radio` creates a radio button that selects its value into a `*T`, with
a label: a click selects it, as does Space while it has the keyboard focus,
and `Changed` reports it. The value can be of any comparable type.

`ui.RadioGroup` holds radio buttons as one stop of Tab: Tab goes to the
one chosen, and the arrows choose among them, as do Home and End.

```go
ui.RadioGroup(c, func() {
	for _, size := range []string{"Small", "Medium", "Large"} {
		ui.Radio(c, &app.size, size, size)
	}
}).Label("Size")
```

A radio group is a column; make it a row with `Row`:

```go
ui.RadioGroup(c, func() {
	ui.Radio(c, &app.align, ui.Start, "Left")
	ui.Radio(c, &app.align, ui.Center, "Center")
	ui.Radio(c, &app.align, ui.End, "Right")
}).Row().Gap(16).Label("Alignment")
```

For a choice among many, use a [select](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/select.md) or a
[combobox](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/combobox.md); between views, a [segmented control](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/segmented.md).

## Without a look

`ui.RadioBase` is a radio button without a look: a row that selects its
value when clicked: see [custom widgets](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/custom-widgets.md).

## Accessibility

Assistive technology sees a radio group named by its `Label`, of radio
buttons named by their labels, on for the one chosen.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/range-slider.md

# Range slider

<!-- preview range-slider 120 -->

`ui.RangeSlider` creates a slider of two knobs setting a low and a high
`*float64` between two bounds, as a price range: each knob takes the
keyboard focus, which Tab moves between, and the arrows, Home and End move
it while it has the focus; a press on the track moves the knob nearest to
it. The knobs do not cross. `Changed` reports a new value.

```go
ui.RangeSlider(c, &app.minPrice, &app.maxPrice, 0, 1000, 10).Label("Price")
ui.Textf(c, "$%.0f – $%.0f", app.minPrice, app.maxPrice)
```

A step above 0 snaps the values to the low bound and multiples of the step
from it, with tick marks; 0 leaves them free.

## Accessibility

Assistive technology sees two sliders, named by the range slider's `Label`
and "minimum" and "maximum".

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/rating.md

# Rating

<!-- preview rating 110 -->

`ui.Rating` creates a row of stars, as AppKit's rating level indicator, of
which an `*int` are filled: a click on a star sets the rating, a click on
the star set clears it, and the arrows, Home and End change it while the
rating has the keyboard focus. `Changed` reports a new value.

```go
ui.Rating(c, &app.stars, 5).Label("Rating")
```

The stars take their size from the theme's font size, and show the rating
a click would set as the pointer rests on them.

## Accessibility

Assistive technology sees a slider from 0 to the number of stars, named by
its `Label`.

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/rendering.md

# Rendering

MyGo draws on the GPU with Metal on macOS, with Direct3D 11 on Windows, or
with WARP, Windows' own software renderer, where no GPU driver works, and
with OpenGL on Linux, in the GtkGLArea GTK shows, and with WebGL 2 in
[browsers](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/browsers.md), with the shader of Linux. A shader computes rounded
rectangles, borders, gradients and shadows from the distance to their
edges, so they stay sharp at any size and scale, and text comes from a
glyph atlas that only uploads what changes.

With a GPU, every frame draws on it. On Linux, the first window of
native UI loads OpenGL: Mesa, the driver, takes some 50 MB, which stay,
about as much as the rest of a small app. Where OpenGL would not run on a
GPU, as in virtual machines or in WSL (where `GALLIUM_DRIVER=d3d12` gives
Mesa the GPU), Linux draws on the CPU: about a millisecond for a whole
large window on a high-density display, on several cores, and less than a
tenth of one for what typically changes, such as a button under the
pointer, since it redraws, and has the compositor take, only that. Set
`MYGO_GPU=0` to use the CPU renderer everywhere, for instance to compare,
and on Linux `MYGO_GPU=1` to draw with OpenGL even where it runs on the
CPU.

Set `MYGO_FRAME_STATS=1` to log each frame that takes longer than 8 ms, or
`MYGO_FRAME_STATS=4` for another threshold in milliseconds (`all` logs
every frame). Each line tells how long building the frame (and in how many
passes), laying it out, painting and presenting it took, whether it was
drawn on the GPU or in memory (where a window has no GPU renderer), what
the process allocated and how many texts it laid out
meanwhile, and whether the garbage collector ran, with the time goroutines
spent helping it mark:

```
mygo: frame 412 took 17.3 ms: build 3.1 (2 passes), layout 1.2, paint 0.8, present 11.5 (drawn on the GPU), other 0.7; meanwhile the process made about 2312 allocations, 171.0 KB, 12 text layouts; GC: 1 cycles ended, 4.1 ms of assists
```

Allocations and the collector are the whole process's, other goroutines'
included, as `runtime/metrics` counts them: a span at a time, so that
small counts read low. While the variable is unset, frames measure
nothing.

MyGo draws a frame only when something changes: input, `Invalidate`,
`After`, or an animation that moves. An idle window draws nothing, and two
seconds after its last frame it frees the frame it drew in memory.

A window animating on macOS keeps three frames for the display, one
more than the two its frames take turns in: with two, a 120 Hz display
holds both often enough that frames wait for one, and some go undrawn.
The third costs about 4 bytes a pixel of the window (8 with colors
outside sRGB) until the window idles.

---

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/rich-text-editor.md

# Rich text editor

<!-- preview rich-text-editor 300 -->

Package `ui/richtext` edits attributed text, as NSTextView does on macOS
and SwiftUI's `TextEditor` bound to an `AttributedString`. It supports:

* **Formats:** bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, inline code, fonts,
  sizes and colors.
* **Links:** opened by a click, and set from the app or with ⌘K.
* **Paragraphs:** headings, bulleted, numbered and task lists,
  quotations, blocks of code and alignment.
* **Attachments:** images inside lines.
* **Editing:** the shortcuts and the Format menu of word processors, and
  undo that brings formats back with the text.
* **Exchange:** copy and paste in rich formats, input methods that compose
  in the typing attributes, Markdown export, and screen readers that
  read the formats.

It lays out and draws only the paragraphs in view, so a long document edits
as a short one.

```go
import "github.com/egoist/mygo/ui/richtext"

// Kept by the app, as its other state.
app.doc = richtext.NewDocument(richtext.NewText("Hello"))

// In the view:
if richtext.Editor(c, app.doc).Fill().Changed() {
	app.save(app.doc.Text())
}
```

The [notes example](https://github.com/egoist/mygo/tree/main/examples/notes) is a notes app with a toolbar, a
link popover and the Format menu, which saves its notes as JSON.

## Text

A `Text` is attributed text: paragraphs, each with a `ParagraphStyle`,
made of runs, each with its `Attributes`. It is a value, as a string is.
Its methods return a new text and leave the one they are called on as it
was, sharing with it all they did not change. Keeping a version, to undo,
to save later or to compare, costs a pointer, and a version can be read
from any goroutine while others are made.

```go
note := richtext.TextOf(
	richtext.Paragraph{Style: richtext.ParagraphStyle{Heading: 1}, Runs: []richtext.Run{{Text: "Groceries"}}},
	richtext.Paragraph{Style: richtext.ParagraphStyle{List: richtext.Tasks}, Runs: []richtext.Run{
		{Text: "Milk, "},
		{Text: "oat", Attributes: richtext.Attributes{Weight: 700}},
	}},
)
note = note.Format(0, 9, func(a *richtext.Attributes) { a.Color = ui.RGB(37, 99, 235) })
note = note.ReplaceString(note.Len(), note.Len(), "\nBread", richtext.Attributes{})
```

Offsets count runes, newlines included, as `Element.TextSelection` does.
To read a text:

* `String` and `PlainText` give its characters;
* `Paragraphs` and `Runs` give its structure;
* `AttributesAt` and `ParagraphStyleAt` describe one rune.

To change one:

* `Replace` and `ReplaceString` change its text;
* `Format` changes the attributes of a range;
* `FormatParagraphs` changes the styles of the paragraphs a range touches.

Attributes left zero take the editor's style: its font, size and color.
`Code`, `Link` and `Tag` (the app's own mark over a run, such as a mention
or a comment) hold only what they hold: text typed at their edges does not
join them.

A paragraph's style and the attributes of its newline belong to the
paragraph, as in word processors: an empty paragraph remembers what typing
gets there. When paragraphs are joined or split, each takes the style of the
paragraph its first rune comes from, as AppKit fixes paragraph styles:

* Deleting the newline after a heading keeps the heading.
* Deleting the heading whole, its newline included, leaves the paragraph
  after it.
* Text pasted at the start of a paragraph brings its own style.

Lists are flat, as in Quill and Automerge: a paragraph's `Indent` is its
level, and items next to each other make a list, numbered at each level from
1 (in letters and Roman numerals below the first).

`MarshalJSON` and `UnmarshalJSON` save a text. `Markdown` and `HTML` export
it, and `ParseMarkdown`, `ParseHTML` and `ParseRTF` read Markdown, HTML and
RTF, as a paste does.

## Documents

A `Document` is what an editor edits: a text, its selection with the
attributes typing gets there, and the history of undo. The app keeps it from
frame to frame. Its methods are safe from any goroutine, so a toolbar, a menu
or a timer formats and edits it while the editor shows it. The editor
follows at its next frame. Schedule changes from other goroutines with
`Window.Update` so that a frame comes.

Commands act on the selection as the editor's shortcuts do. On a range,
they change its runs or paragraphs as one step of undo. On a caret,
character formats change only the typing attributes, which the next typed
text gets and the next move of the caret forgets, as ⌘B does in NSTextView.

```go
f := app.doc.Formatting() // the selection's formats, for a toolbar
bold := ui.Button(c, "B")
if f.Bold == richtext.FormatOn {
	bold.Background(t.Accent.Alpha(0.18))
}
if bold.KeepFocus().Clicked() {
	app.doc.ToggleBold()
}
```

`Formatting` gives each character format as `FormatOn`, `FormatOff` or
`FormatMixed`, along with the link the selection is in and the style of its
first paragraph. These methods change the document:

| Method                                                                                                     | What it does                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `ToggleBold`, `ToggleItalic`, `ToggleUnderline`, `ToggleStrikethrough`, `ToggleCode`                       | turns a format on, or off when all of the selection has it                               |
| `Format(fn)`                                                                                               | changes any attribute, as a font, a size or a color                                      |
| `SetLink(url)`                                                                                             | links the selection, the link at the caret, or inserts the URL; `""` takes the link away |
| `SetHeading(level)`, `ToggleList(kind)`, `ToggleQuote`, `ToggleCodeBlock`, `Indent(levels)`, `SetAlign(a)` | change the paragraphs selected                                                           |
| `FormatParagraphs(fn)`                                                                                     | changes any paragraph style                                                              |
| `ToggleChecked(i)`                                                                                         | checks the task holding rune `i`                                                         |
| `InsertText`, `Insert`, `InsertAttachment`                                                                 | replace the selection                                                                    |
| `Edit(fn)`                                                                                                 | changes it any way, as one step of undo                                                  |
| `Undo`, `Redo`, `BreakUndoCoalescing`                                                                      | take steps back and forth                                                                |
| `SetText`                                                                                                  | replaces the text, as opening another note, and clears the history                       |

`Edit` runs a function on an `Edit`, whose `Replace`, `ReplaceString`,
`Format`, `FormatParagraphs` and `Select` change the document as one step of
undo. The selection follows what changes, as AttributedString tracks
indices: a caret where text is inserted goes after it, and a range does not
grow at its end.

```go
app.doc.Edit(func(e *richtext.Edit) {
	e.ReplaceString(0, 0, "Dear Ann,\n", richtext.Attributes{})
	e.Format(0, 8, func(a *richtext.Attributes) { a.Italic = true })
})
```

## The editor

`Editor` is the editor with the look of a text area: padding, a background,
a border and corners. `EditorBase` has none of these, for an editor of the
app's own look.

`Changed` reports the edits the user made in the editor, not those the app
made through the document. `EditorOptions` set:

* `Label` and `Placeholder`;
* `Font`, the editor's font and size;
* `ReadOnly`, a text the user selects, copies, and clicks the links of;
* `NoMarkdown`, which turns the Markdown shortcuts off;
* `OnLink`, to open links itself instead of the system;
* `OnLinkCommand`, to ask for a link's URL on ⌘K, as in a popover;
* `TagStyle`, to style the runs that carry a `Tag`.
* `Theme`, how the text looks (see [Theme](#theme)).

The keys are those of word processors, with Control in place of Command off
macOS:

| Key                           | macOS                            | Windows and Linux           |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Bold, italic, underline       | ⌘B, ⌘I, ⌘U                       | Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+U      |
| Strikethrough                 | ⇧⌘X                              | Ctrl+Shift+X                |
| Code                          | ⌘E                               | Ctrl+Shift+E                |
| Link                          | ⌘K                               | Ctrl+K                      |
| Numbered, bulleted, task list | ⇧⌘7, ⇧⌘8, ⇧⌘L                    | Ctrl+Shift+7, 8, L          |
| Indent, outdent               | ⌘], ⌘\[ (Tab and ⇧Tab in a list) | Ctrl+], Ctrl+\[             |
| Align left, center, right     | ⌘{, ⌘\|, ⌘}                      | Ctrl+L, Ctrl+E, Ctrl+R      |
| Heading 1 to 6, body          | ⌥⌘1 to ⌥⌘6, ⌥⌘0                  | Ctrl+Alt+1 to 6, Ctrl+Alt+0 |
| Previous, next paragraph      | ⌥↑, ⌥↓                           | Ctrl+↑, Ctrl+↓              |
| Start, end of the text        | ⌘↑, ⌘↓                           | Ctrl+Home, Ctrl+End         |

Paragraphs behave as in Notes and Google Docs:

* Enter continues a list, and on an empty item leaves it.
* Enter at the end of a heading starts a body paragraph.
* Backspace at the start of a list's item, a heading, a quotation or a
  block of code takes the style away before joining the paragraph to the
  one above.
* A click on a task's check box checks it, and a click on a link opens it:
  an `http`, `https` or `mailto` address (`ui.SafeToOpen`), as Markdown
  views open them, since other schemes and paths run programs on Windows.
  `OnLink` opens links itself instead.

The Markdown shortcuts format what is typed: at the start of a paragraph,
`# ` to `###### ` make headings, `- `, `* ` and `+ ` bulleted lists, `1. `
numbered ones, `[ ] ` and `[x] ` tasks, `> ` a quotation, and ` ``` `
then Enter a block of code. Around words, `**bold**`, `*italic*`,
`_italic_`, `` `code` `` and `~~strikethrough~~` format what they hold as the
closing mark is typed; an underscore inside a word, as in `snake_case`,
stays one. Undo takes a shortcut back to what was typed.

The [Format menu's roles](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/menus.md#roles) (`RoleFormatMenu`, or
`RoleBold`, `RoleAlignCenter`, …) format the editor with the keyboard
focus. Paste and Match Style pastes plain text in the typing attributes.

## Theme

`EditorOptions.Theme` sets how the text looks: the colors of text, muted
text, links, the caret and the selection; the font, size and colors of
code, within text and in blocks, and the corners and room of blocks of
code; each level of heading's size, weight, color and room above and
below; the indentation of lists, the colors of their markers and check
boxes; the bar and text of quotations; and the padding of `Editor`,
which replaces the window theme's. What it leaves zero takes the
value of `DefaultTheme` for the window's theme, so that a theme sets only
what it changes, and follows the window into dark mode:

```go
violet := ui.Hex("#7c3aed")
richtext.Editor(c, doc, richtext.EditorOptions{Theme: &richtext.Theme{
	Link:     violet,
	Checkbox: violet,
	Headings: [6]richtext.HeadingStyle{{Size: 2.2, Weight: 800}},
}})
```

Lengths are in ems, times the editor's font size, so that a theme scales
with `Font`, but for the padding and the quotation bar's width, in DIPs. Changing the theme lays the text out again. The colors the
editor shows go to screen readers with its runs.

## Typing at the edges of formats

Text typed takes the attributes of the character before the caret. At the
start of a paragraph it takes those of the character after it, and in place
of a selection those of the first character selected. These are NSTextView's
rules, measured on macOS 27, and those of ProseMirror, Lexical and Quill:

* Typing at the end of bold continues bold; at its start, it does not.
* Typing at the end of a link, a code span or a tag does not continue it.
  Inside one, it does.
* After the text before the caret is deleted, typing gets its attributes
  until the caret moves: delete a bold word and type, and the text is bold.
* After Enter, typing keeps the attributes typed before it.

## Attachments

An attachment is an object replacement character (U+FFFC) whose
`Attributes.Attachment` holds an `Attachment`: an image, or a drawing of the
app's, laid out as a box inside the line, standing on the baseline. It is
selected, copied and deleted as one character, and lines break around it.
A box wider than the editor is scaled down to fit.

```go
photo, _ := ui.DecodeBitmap(data)
app.doc.InsertAttachment(&richtext.Attachment{Image: photo, Name: "Beach", Width: 240})
```

Without an image or a `Draw` function, an attachment shows its `Name` in a
box, as an image not loaded yet. HTML and Markdown write an attachment's
`URL`.

## Copy and paste

Copying puts the selection on the clipboard in three formats:

* the editor's own (`richtext.Format`, JSON), which MyGo apps paste whole,
  attachments included within the app;
* HTML;
* plain text.

Pasting reads the richest format the clipboard holds: the editor's own,
then HTML, then RTF, then Markdown (`transfer.Markdown`, which Markdown
views and apps copy), then plain text. A [Markdown view](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/markdown.md)'s
selection pastes with its formatting.

* HTML, as browsers, mail, Word and Google Docs copy it, keeps its
  headings, lists, task lists, quotations, blocks of code, alignment,
  bold, italic, underline, strikethrough, code and links.
* RTF, as TextEdit, Pages and WordPad copy it without HTML, keeps its
  paragraphs, alignment, lists, bold, italic, underline, strikethrough and
  links. Fonts, sizes and colors are left out, as
  Notes leaves them, so that what is pasted takes the editor's. Paste and
  Match Style (⇧⌥⌘V) pastes plain text in the typing attributes.

## Input methods

An input method composes at the caret in the typing attributes, as AppKit
and Qt show it, underlined while it composes. The whole composition is one
step of undo with what it replaced.

## Accessibility

Screen readers read the editor as a text field, with the formats of its
runs:

* **VoiceOver** reads `AXAttributedStringForRange`: fonts, colors,
  underlines, strikethroughs and links.
* **Orca** reads ATK's run attributes.
* **Narrator** reads UI Automation's Text pattern, by characters, formats,
  words and lines, with the font, weight, italics, lines, colors and
  heading level of each run, and the mixed value where they vary.

Screen readers move the selection too.

## Large documents

The text is a rope of chunks with a persistent sequence of paragraphs beside
it, so an edit copies what it touches and the path to it, and costs
O(log n). The editor lays out only the paragraphs in view, keeps the layouts
of those near it, and estimates the heights of the others. Typing a
character in a document of 100,000 formatted paragraphs, and drawing the
frame on the CPU, takes about as long as in one of 1,000 (`BenchmarkTypeFrame`
in `ui/richtext`).

## Markdown

`Text.Markdown` writes CommonMark with GitHub's extensions:

* headings, lists, task lists, quotations and fenced blocks of code;
* `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `~~strikethrough~~`, `` `code` ``, links and
  images;
* underlines as `<u>`, and as `<strong>`, `<em>` and `<del>` the marks
  that Markdown's delimiters cannot open or close where they are, as bold
  "foo." right before "bar".

Alignment, fonts and colors have no Markdown and are left out.

`ParseMarkdown` reads it back, and what a model or another app wrote:
CommonMark with GitHub's extensions and footnotes, with the parser of
[Markdown views](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/markdown.md) (`ui/markdown/parser`). A list item's
paragraphs after its first are indented under it, and a table's rows are
paragraphs of their cells apart by tabs. Math stays as written, as the
editor does not show it. What `Markdown` writes reads back the same.

Source: https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/right-to-left.md

# Right to left

Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and Urdu read from right to left, and so do the
interfaces of apps in those languages: a row starts at the right, a
sidebar is on the right, a back arrow points right. Native UI lays a window
out so when the app's language reads right to left, as Flutter's
`Directionality`, SwiftUI's `layoutDirection`, CSS's `direction` and GTK's
text direction do. The coordinate system is not mirrored, as in Godot:
X still grows to the right in `Rect`, in what `Draw` paints, and in the
pointer's position. Only the layout is.

## The direction

`ui.LeftToRight` and `ui.RightToLeft` are the two directions
(`ui.Direction`). A window takes the direction of the app's language,
which package `mygo` gives it, and every element that of the element it is
built in. `Direction` gives an element and what is built inside it a
direction of their own, as a phone number, a code sample or a media
player's controls that stay left to right in a right-to-left window:

```go
ui.Row(c).Direction(ui.LeftToRight).Gap(8).Children(func() {
	ui.Button(c, "⏮")
	ui.Button(c, "⏯")
	ui.Button(c, "⏭")
})
```

Give it right after creating the element, before its children, as you
would `Key`: widgets read the direction as they are built. The popups
attached to an element (popovers, comboboxes' options, tooltips) and what
an `Overlay` builds take the direction of where they were asked for.

`Context.Direction` returns the direction of what is built now, for
widgets of your own that draw what points along the line:

```go
forward := "M5 2 11 8 5 14"
if c.Direction() == ui.RightToLeft {
	forward = "M11 2 5 8 11 14"
}
```

## What mirrors

Right to left:

* A `Row` lays its children out from the right, and a `Column` aligns them
  across from the right: `Justify`, `AlignItems` and `AlignSelf` take
  `Start` and `End` from the direction. `Reverse` lays a row out from the
  left. A grid places its columns from the right, and `JustifyItems` and
  `JustifySelf` start at the right of their cells.
* `TextAlign`'s `Start` is the right of the element, whatever its text
  reads, as in CSS, AppKit and GTK, and `End` the left. A paragraph reads
  in the direction of its first strongly directional character, as Unicode's
  bidirectional algorithm finds it, and one without any, as a number or an
  empty line, right to left. Left to right, nothing changes: a paragraph
  in Arabic still starts at the right, as Apple's guidelines align a
  paragraph by its language.
* The logical edges are on the right where they start: `PaddingStart`,
  `PaddingEnd`, `MarginStart`, `MarginEnd`, `BorderStartWidth`,
  `BorderEndWidth`, the `Start` and `End` of positioned elements (and
  `StartPercent`, `EndPercent`), and the anchors `AnchorTopStart`,
  `AnchorStart`, `AnchorBottomStart`, `AnchorTopEnd`, `AnchorEnd` and
  `AnchorBottomEnd`, as CSS's logical properties and Flutter's
  `EdgeInsetsDirectional` and `AlignmentDirectional`. An absolute element
  placed from neither side goes to the right, and where both `Left` and
  `Right` are given and its width leaves no room for both, `Right` wins.
* Scrolling sideways starts at the right, and `ScrollState.X` counts from
  there (0 shows the start, `MaxX` the end), as Flutter's offsets do; the
  wheel and the trackpad move the content as they do left to right, and
  Shift with the wheel goes toward the end. The vertical scroll bar is on
  the left.
* The controls mirror what points along the line: a switch turns on to
  the left; sliders, range sliders, progress bars and meters fill from the
  right, and their arrows move the knob the way they point; tabs,
  segmented controls, toolbars, ratings, grid views and calendars go to
  their next item with Left; disclosure arrows, breadcrumbs' chevrons, a
  toolbar's overflow and the back button point left, or right for back;
  trees, outlines and disclosures indent from the right and open with
  Left; a split's first pane is on the right; a table's columns go from
  the right and resize from their left edges; pages pushed on a router
  slide in from the left, and Alt+Right goes back.
* Popovers, a select's and a combobox's options, and the menus of menu
  buttons open at the start of what opens them, and context menus are laid
  out right to left, opening to the left of the pointer.
* In a single-line text input, the text starts at the right, its
  placeholder too, and the caret of an empty one is there. The arrows move
  the caret the way they point, through text of either direction, and
  Option (Control elsewhere) and Command with the arrows go by words and to
  line ends the way they point in a right-to-left paragraph, as AppKit and
  GTK do.

## What does not

* What is physical stays physical, as in CSS: `Left`, `Right`,
  `Padding(top, right, bottom, left)`, `BorderWidth`, `AnchorTopLeft`,
  `Radius`'s corners, gradients' angles, transforms.
* Text, images, icons and what `Draw` paints are not mirrored: a check
  mark, a magnifying glass, a spinner and a chart read as they do left to
  right. Draw what must point the other way after reading
  `Context.Direction`.
* Code reads left to right: the code editor and the diff viewer
  (`ui/editor`), Markdown's code blocks and the terminal keep their own
  direction, as do time inputs, as times are written so.
* The rich text editor (`ui/richtext`) aligns its paragraphs as their text
  reads, as a document does.
* The inspector reads left to right.

## Trying it

`MYGO_DIRECTION=rtl` lays every window of native UI out right to left
(and `ltr` left to right), whatever the app's language, to try an
interface before it is translated, as GTK's `GTK_DEBUG=invert-text-dir`
and Qt's `-reverse` do:

```sh
MYGO_DIRECTION=rtl mygo dev
```

The [inspector](https://mygo.egoist.dev/docs/ui/inspector.md)'s RTL toggle does the same for its window
while it runs, and a `Tester` lays its window out right to left after
`SetDirection(ui.RightToLeft)`, as a test of the layout would:

```go
tt := ui.NewTester(app.view, 400, 300)
tt.SetDirection(ui.RightToLeft)
back, _ := tt.Find("Back")
if back.X < 200 {
	t.Error("the back button is not at the right")
}
```

The [gallery](https://github.com/egoist/mygo/tree/main/examples/gallery) shows every control right to left
with the toggle in its toolbar.
